An area of study called 'Web 2.0 personalisation research' analyzes the influence of customisation techniques used by information systems on users' perception of available data. Our study focuses on the extent of relevant content that is overlooked due to a customised presentation of search results on Google's platform. We employed a laboratory-based experiment where participants conducted same searches both on Google in their normal browsing habit and in an unbiased manner. The findings revealed that a considerable proportion of users (in excess of 50%) fail to discover top-ranked search results when personalised recommendations are involved. Moreover, it was observed that up to 30% of users may miss key information when relying solely on customised search results. These outcomes highlight the potential drawbacks of personalisation and customisation practices used by information systems and suggest a need for greater transparency and informed consent from users. On a parallel note, these results present opportunities for theoretical and empirical advancements in the field of Web 2.0 personalisation research. The current study is the first to provide empirical evidence of both direct and indirect influences of customisation on users' comprehension of available data. By distinction, prior studies had addressed the quantity of content but not its quality, while also raising ethical and practical concerns about customisation practices. Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel approach called graph synthesis involves translating flow chart diagrams into executable code. Previous methods using graph grammars and evolutionary algorithms have encountered difficulties in their implementations, and have so far failed to generate functional Java code from the Harvard Stepic course dataset. A new method called GRCNN has been developed, leveraging a convolutional neural network to analyze and translate the elements within these diagrams into meaningful Java code. Through thorough testing, GRCNN has successfully generated functional Java code from the Harvard Stepic course dataset. Additionally, when provided with diagrams representing recursive string functions, GRCNN has demonstrated the ability to learn and generate correct code even when the input diagrams contain synthetic obstacles. A comparison against state-of-the-art graph synthesis systems has shown that GRCNN's generated code is preferred by human evaluators over the alternative methods. The loss of close-in massive planets around old stars in the solar neighborhood has long been a subject of study. Based on the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity sample from $0.4\,M_{\earth}$ to $10\,M_{\earth}$ and $0.1\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ to $1\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, a comprehensive analysis was conducted to investigate this phenomenon. After detecting $183$ planets with semimajor axes below $4\,\mathrm{AU}$ and masses greater than $0.3\,M_{\earth}$, it was possible to place constraints on the planar metallicity distribution. As a result, it was found that super-Earths and Neptune-mass planets with masses between $0.3\,M_{\earth}$ and $10\,M_{\earth}$ are significantly more abundant around metal-rich stars. These stars are also more likely to host multiple planets. This trend persists even after controlling for detection biases. Our study suggests that there is no evidence to support the notion of a "planetary desert" around $1\,M_{\earth}$ or $4\,\mathrm{AU}$ in the sample considered. Rather, it was found that radial velocity detection biases may contribute to the perceived absence of massive planets around metal-poor stars close to their host stars. As telescopes become more sensitive, it is possible that the planetary desert will be explored in greater detail. Future observations using the ELT and its potential for direct imaging may reveal the presence of a massive planet around a metal-poor star every few astronomical units from its host star, particularly if these planets have smaller orbital periods and masses above $0.1\,M_{\earth}$. It is also possible that such planets have escaped from their orbital orbits around metal-poor stars. As a result, it is possible that the planetary desert may be attributed to planets with smaller masses rather than those with larger masses. This study confirms that radial velocity detection biases may contribute to the perceived absence of massive planets around metal-poor stars. As a result, it is possible that the planetary desert may be attributed to planets with smaller masses rather than those with larger masses. To confirm this theory, it is necessary to conduct additional observations of planets with smaller masses using the ELT and its potential for direct imaging. If this theory is confirmed, it is necessary to reevaluate the presence of a massive planet around metal-poor stars.

This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry, yielding more robust results under partial overlap and varying lighting conditions. Building on the success of Symmetry-Permutation (SP)-based feature extensions, our research focuses on the development of a novel, real-valued 3D feature descriptor rooted in SP-invariance. As a result, these features are insensitive to image symmetry and the sequence in which they are applied. In addition to feature enhancement, our work contributes an advanced image registration technique combining SP-invariant features with the Simplex optimization algorithm, producing more accurate results, particularly with low overlap and varying lighting conditions. Our findings demonstrate the superiority of SP-invariant features over their rigid and translation-invariant counterparts and, when used for image registration, achieve higher mean similarity scores, as evidenced by our experiments on three public datasets. The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the unification theory for different types of Active Galactic Nuclei. By collecting and analyzing a large dataset of 853 Active Galactic Nuclei, a comprehensive study was conducted to compare various characteristics of their host galaxies. This study employed three distinct types of Active Galactic Nuclei: Blue, Type 1, and Flat Plateau, each exhibiting distinct optical spectral features, and found that they have distinct relationships with their host galaxies. Specifically, the findings reveal that the galaxies associated with the Blue type actively grow and have higher star formation rates, characterized by higher Hα luminosity ratios and bluer colors. In contrast, the galaxies associated with Type 1 and Flat Plateau Active Galactic Nuclei show little evidence of star formation and have slower growth rates. Furthermore, the findings of this study suggest that the orientation of jet activity in Flat Plateau Active Galactic Nuclei is significantly different from that of Type 1 and Blue Active Galactic Nuclei. This observation is supported by previous studies of Flat Plateau Active Galactic Nuclei, which have noted the absence of flaring in jet spectra. Based on these results, it is proposed that Flat Plateau Active Galactic Nuclei may be characterized by a unique, compact radio structure and are likely to be located in a specific environment that facilitates star formation in host galaxies. Finally, the findings of this study also suggest that Flat Plateau Active Galactic Nuclei may be an intermediate state in the development of Blazars. This theory is supported by a comparison of key characteristics of Flat Plateau Active Galactic Nuclei with those of Blazars. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the relationships between Active Galactic Nuclei and their host galaxies and offers a new perspective on the classification of Active Galactic Nuclei. This research may also be used to develop statistical selection methods for Blazar and Flat Plateau Active Galactic Nuclei using optical spectral features. This study also lays the groundwork for a new classification framework for Active Galactic Nuclei that is based on optical spectral features. This framework, which was used to conduct the study, includes four main types: Blue, Type 1, Flat Plateau, and Core-Dominant Active Galactic Nuclei. This classification framework is consistent with the traditional Sy, BL Lac, and FGK quasar classifications, and may be used in future studies. especially when limited labeled data is available. In recent years, various methods have been developed for pre-training on independent datasets. The rise of autonomous vehicles and health monitoring depends heavily on interpreting vessel equipment data, which includes faulty and missing measurement values that must be addressed. Current methods in time-series narration focus solely on uncovering patterns (e.g., hidden states, hierarchical relationships), but neglect the core task of describing temporal connections between items. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a novel neural model that can handle missing and faulty measurement values and accurately predict temporal relationships. TCube leverages a dual representation learning framework, which learns item-specific and shared features separately for enhanced representation learning. Additionally, TCube incorporates an attention-based message passing layer to capture long-term temporal patterns and the relative importance of individual measurements. Evaluation on three real-world datasets reveals that TCube consistently outperforms existing methods in precision and recall by significant margins. Notably, TCube improves recall by 11.6% and 16.3% on two datasets, and significantly reduces errors in predicted temporal connections by 87.3%. Notably, the experiment has found evidence of CP violation in the decay of the B0s meson for the first time ever. Additionally, the ATLAS team has set new records for detecting extremely rare events, such as the decay of the B meson into a muon and an anti-tau particle, and the decay of the B0s meson into one muon and another muon. The experiment has also established new limits on the occurrence of another rare process, the decay of the B0 meson into one muon and an anti-tau particle. This study explores the well-posedness of a first-order quasilinearity, high-order variational phase space hyperbolic PDE with sublogarithmic coefficients in time. Our research reveals that the given problem has a unique and globally continuous solution for various classes of smooth initial conditions, even when the coefficients have moderate smoothness. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the solution remains stable in $H^2_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ when the initial condition has $H^2$ smoothness. One notable example that fits this category is a phase field equation describing a thermodynamic process, which shows that the solution is not only continuous but also converges to the corresponding Euler equations' solution at a certain rate. Our proof relies on an established method for similar problems, which involves constructing a suitable barried problem and applying a suitable energy type estimate. On the other hand, our example also highlights the significance of considering the specific growth rates of coefficients in the study of hyperbolic PDEs. To conclude, our study supplements and broadens the existing results for a specific type of hyperbolic PDE with sublogarithmic coefficients, which were published in the journal Mathematical Methods and Applications. Additionally, our study initiates new directions for future research by inspiring inquiries about the well-posedness of more complex equations involving higher-order derivatives and complex geometries. Future research could also involve considering the pointwise estimates of solutions, rather than local energy estimates, which could provide more precise and valuable insights into the behavior of solutions. Another potential area of inquiry is the development of a suitable suitable condition for the phase space hyperbolic PDE, which could help establish the global well-posedness of the original problem, even for large initial conditions. Finally, we conjecture that the solution of the original problem would either converge to a steady state or a periodic solution, depending on the sign of a certain parameter value, which could be confirmed by combining the properties of the Euler equations' solution and the vanishing viscosity method. These potential research avenues not only build upon our study but also encourage further investigation of the interplay between dynamics and geometry. To facilitate this, we have introduced a novel perspective on the pointwise behavior of solutions (see the discussion section for more information). This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese term segmentation. Traditional character-based models often fall short in accurately separating characters, particularly in certain character combinations. In contrast, our proposed LSTM model leverages contextual information to enhance performance. Additionally, our study identifies and addresses a limitation in existing LSTM models based on character-level word embeddings, leading to improved accuracy and computational efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model over existing methods on a substantial Japanese corpus, encompassing 1.2 billion words. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that character-level word embeddings are advantageous over previous models using word-level embeddings. Notably, our best-performing model achieved a character error rate of 59.6, marking a significant improvement over state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, this research presents a novel adaptation of the FastText's supervised learning framework to enhance LSTM's training. This technique, using subword information, facilitates the modeling of rare and unknown word aspects. Also, our study introduces a character-based FastText model, demonstrating superior performance over existing methods. All our experimental code and models have been made publicly available for reference and replication of results. This research aims to contribute to the advancement of Japanese term segmentation, particularly in character-level models, and also addresses related challenges in other languages with complex writing systems. In a related effort, our study also applies the LSTM model to the tasks of Japanese part-of-speech tagging and sentence parsing. This study aims to enhance the understanding of random forests by drawing comparisons with individual decision trees. This paper introduces a novel method, called Timeloops, to automatically generate decision-making algorithms for system call policies in containerized microservices. Current approaches to ensuring microservice security rely heavily on the examination of system calls. However, implementing a customized system call enforcement mechanism for each microservice is a complex task. These policies can then be easily integrated into the existing Linux kernel. Our framework's performance benefits have been demonstrated through a combination of theoretical and practical studies, which found that it surpasses traditional static-based approaches in terms of efficiency and flexibility. Ultimately, our research seeks to promote a more adaptable and dynamic approach to ensuring microservice security, poised to meet the evolving demands of users and environments. We've analyzed the long-term dynamics of stars orbiting close to a supermassive black hole using N-body simulations, focusing on a strong separation regime where tidal forces are significant. Our models showed a natural emergence of distinct stellar populations, separated by critical boundaries in orbital energy and angular momentum. The innermost population, consisting of highly eccentric stars, follows a predictable trajectory, eventually being ejected from the galaxy. The other populations, with lower eccentricities and orbital radii, are found to have a natural separation rate, leading to a long-term steady state. Specifically, we identified a intermediate population with high orbital probability, confirming previous N-body findings. In contrast, we found a lack of support for a theoretical "island" population with highly inclined orbits for the given tidal radius case. However, we suggest this population could be formed if the supermassive black hole expands due to gas accretion, thereby increasing the tidal radius. Our results have implications for observing and understanding the past and future histories of stellar distributions in galaxies, especially those with active galactic nuclei. Moreover, we emphasize the importance of accounting for tidal disruption rates in modeling galactic populations, rather than assuming they remain constant over time. Notably, an intermediate period of population decline may occur before species recovery, even if the species' long-term invasion rate remains positive.  The impact of disruption (demographic stochasticity) on these communities is particularly pronounced and may favor the survival of diverse populations, while significantly lowering the risk of global homogenization (population extinction).  Our conclusions are bolstered by numerical simulations, yet also highlight the inherent challenge of accurately predicting critical community thresholds due to the sudden, abrupt nature of demographic transitions. We demonstrate that the patterns defined by set inclusion maintain the expansion property, whereas those defined by propositional equivalence do not. Additionally, we discuss the relevance of this property to the generalized concept of $t\dot x$-substitutions, connecting it to the concept of $t$-interpretations. Furthermore, we discuss the solvability of systems of equations through $t$-interpretations, revealing a connection to the expansion property. We also introduce the concept of semi-expansions and demonstrate its equivalence to a specific type of $t$-interpretation, called simplicial interpretations, in models where relations have at most three elements. We conclude by highlighting a particular model satisfying all conditions but having a relation with four elements, thereby contradicting a previously established theorem. Finally, we show the separation between set inclusion and propositional equivalence patterns through a specific counterexample. Building on previous work, a powerful approach has been developed for making inferences and predicting new data in a targeted subspace of a high-dimensional space. This method builds upon previous research in predictive inference and subspace modeling, integrating projection predictive control and predictive learning concepts. It offers several key advantages over existing techniques: it can handle non-Gaussian systems; data from these systems can be predicted; and the impact of high dimensional variables can be managed effectively; and the approach is easy to implement. Two applications of this method are explored in detail: a synthetic dataset and a real-world dataset from the field of medicine. This method is now being made available through an open-source package called PPControl. 

This work is inspired by the theories of predictive learning and subspace modeling. It draws on previous research in these fields, integrating it with the concept of predictive inference known as prediction interval estimation. This new approach shares some characteristics with existing predictive methods such as Bayesian predictive distributions and predictive learning, but it is distinct from them in significant ways. 

The core concept of this method is rooted in a statistical framework that involves making inferences about a targeted subspace of a high-dimensional space based on a sample of data. This is done through two key processes called projection and predictive inference. When a new observation is predicted, the data is first transformed into the targeted subspace through a projection operation, and then a predictive distribution is generated based on this transformed data. 

The technique is known as Latent Space Projection Predictive Estimation, and it is characterized by four main variables: two that define the targeted subspace and two that govern the structure of the data. These variables are estimated efficiently using an approach based on Monte-Carlo sampling. This method is now being made available through an open-source package called PPControl. 

Two applications of this method are explored in detail: a synthetic dataset and a real-world dataset from the field of medicine. The former is used to demonstrate how predictions can be made effectively using data from the same population, while the latter is used to show how predictions can be made effectively using data from a different population. 

In particular, the real-world dataset is based on research on a type of fungus that affects grapevines, and it is used to make inferences and predict new data in a space that is targeted specifically to compare the effects of different variables. The results show that this method allows for the interpretation of inferences and predictions in a common language, and it is now being made available through an open-source package called PPControl.

This type of attack involves intercepting data communications, then manipulating them with malicious generated data to deceive machine learning based systems. Our study investigates this sophisticated attack on 2D and 3D object detection algorithms and a facial attribute analysis model, revealing that all these systems are susceptible to its effects. This type of attack poses significant risks particularly to industries in transition such as those transitioning from rule-based to data-driven methods. It can significantly undermine trust in machine learning based applications if they fail to account for this type of threat and implement secure communication protocols. Our findings show that an attacker can launch this attack by utilizing existing malicious models fine-tuned for adversarial purposes. To carry out the attack, the attacker must intercept the request, modify it with the malicious data, and have it transmitted back to the victim, a process that can be hindered by secure protocols but is otherwise highly effective in a variety of settings. It turns out that a relatively small number of modified samples can substantially reduce the effectiveness of the machine learning model. This type of attack could potentially be launched against a wide range of machine learning models and applications, and what is more it appears that traditional machine learning based systems are just as vulnerable to it as deep learning based ones. Climate denial theories disseminated via social networks pose a threat to public perception, and the spread of misinformation about climate change via social media platforms demands attention. Existing research into climate deniers has focused on their online activities, but this study investigates the underlying characteristics of climate deniers who spread misinformation on Twitter. By analyzing Twitter data linked to prominent climate conspiracy theorists, researchers identified climate deniers' core beliefs and their dissemination of misinformation. Further analysis revealed that a small group of highly active users drives the spread of climate conspiracy theories, and that climate deniers are primarily right-wing and consistently apply the same conspiracy theories across various topics. Furthermore, targeting these spreaders of misinformation and addressing the underlying structural factors could be crucial in mitigating the impact of climate conspiracy theories. Ultimately, the research implies that efforts to counter climate conspiracy theories on Twitter should focus on the individuals who consistently disseminate such misinformation. These users tend to hold extreme ideological views and rely on the same conspiracy theories in relation to multiple topics, and addressing these spreaders may be key to effectively addressing the problem. Information intervention strategies, such as labeling, ranking, and banning users, may be useful in reducing the dissemination of climate conspiracy theories. Conversely, focusing on correcting user posts may be an ineffective approach, and it is also essential to address the underlying structural factors that enable the spread of conspiracy theories through social media. translated into images. The framework comprises three modules: an generator,
adversarial discriminator, and auxiliary classifier. The generator module is a
deep learning network that converts low-quality document images into high-resolution
images. The adversarial discriminator monitors the generated images to ensure they
appear legitimate and authentic, primarily focusing on text presented in a normal
state. Meanwhile, the auxiliary classifier module assists the generator by providing

considerable margin, 14.3% and 9.5% respectively, when tested on the same dataset.

SSIM. The effectiveness of this model was verified through both qualitative and
quantitative analysis of the restored text and its compatibility with existing
text recognition tools. Notably, the same model can also be utilized for restoring
handwritten documents, thereby expanding its potential practical applications.

We propose introducing causal knowledge to adaptative methods through the implementation of semi-generative models, integrating both cause and effect features into a single training process. These models can be viewed as a combination of causal generative adversarial networks, with the advantage of being globally applicable, as they do not rely on specific causal models. By drawing from entropic measurements, our method offers a more comprehensive solution to covariate-shift adaptation, as it learns to adjust policies and generate cause features while matching both cause and effect distributions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in complex, high-dimensional environments and highlight its ability to be adaptable to diverse causal models. Moreover, our method exhibits a more substantial gain in performance over traditional reward shaping and importance sampling techniques. We also show that our semi-generative models can be applied to reinforcement learning domains where the reward is not fully known in advance. The use of Virtual Reality technology is increasingly widespread, and it is expected that its adoption will continue to grow. Researchers are now focusing on the psychological and social implications of its development and use. Some of the most fundamental challenges come from the fact that users often experience discrepancies between their perceptions and reality. These perceptual distortions can take many forms, resulting in users' altered sense of time and space, and even affecting their memory and behavior. The aim of this paper is to provide an overview of the current state of research on the darker aspects of Virtual Reality technologies and their applications. We are examining the following topics: the relationship between time and reality, spatial perception, memory distortion, and the blurred lines between reality and imagination. We are also exploring the potential risks and consequences of VR use in various fields, such as psychology, law, medicine, and social sciences. In the end, we present the current state of knowledge and highlight the need for further research in the future. Series of studies are planned to be conducted to investigate the very dark side of Virtual Reality. The studies aim at understanding the impact of VR perceptions on users' behavior and judgment, and whether such an impact can be manipulated by third parties. The proposed research has the potential to contribute significantly to the field of social sciences, and can serve as a guide for industry professionals and policymakers. By examining the relationship between VR perceptions and behavior, we aim to gain insights into the ways in which VR can be used to influence people's decisions, and whether such an influence can be traced back to the distortions in their perceptions. The research will provide valuable practical knowledge that can be used to shape people's attitudes towards VR, and can be applied in various areas such as law enforcement and medicine. The study will also address a number of ethical and theoretical issues, and will shed light on the role of perceptions in shaping behavior, as well as the ways in which VR can be used to manipulate people's actions. Finally, the paper will explore the future of VR research from a philosophical and predictive point of view. To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into the renowned BigScience multilingual language model, pre-trained on the Internet Archive's content. Our study investigates three methods for adding new languages to a model: (1) fine-tuning existing transformers with language-specific masked language modeling, (2) generating new vocabulary with language-specific word prediction, and (3) reconstructing the model's internal language representation using custom transformation modules. We evaluate these strategies' effectiveness in improving models' understanding of new languages, specifically German and Korean, as well as generalizing to similar languages, such as Dutch and Swedish. Our results show that fine-tuning and the word prediction method consistently enhance models' performance in zero-shot settings, while the transformation module approach excels in adapting new language vocabulary. Notably, the BigScience model exhibits high levels of performance in zero-shot language understanding tasks, achieving 82.5% F1 score on German and 85.5% F1 score on Korean on NER benchmarks. Our research also identifies room for improvement in existing transformer architectures' adaptability to new languages and proposes various optimizations for future models. Finally, our code and model repositories are publicly available for other researchers to reproduce and build upon our findings. Our analysis focuses on the capabilities of these systems in capturing the semantics of first-order logic, with CPT being particularly interesting due to its inability to fully capture even the properties of ordered trees. Our key contribution lies in developing a new methodology for showing the limitations of CPT and related PC systems. This involves constructing distinct structures in specific domains that cannot be differentiated by certain logic-based systems. Conversely, although CPT is capable of capturing properties of ordered trees, its absolute consistency cannot be established through model counting and related techniques. Former claims of reaching human-level chess play were examined in the 1980s, and it is revealed that the path to achieving this goal involved specific, incremental advancements within the search framework of chess. It is contemplated that a comparable, systematic approach may hold value for advancing AI development, particularly in areas like NLP where significant breakthroughs thus far lack a unifying theory. By analyzing the process of developing search frameworks in computer programs, researchers might identify a universal language for creating successful AI systems, thereby identifying potential deficits in current methods such as lacking structured input and output options for guiding search efforts. It is posited that focusing on enhancing search frameworks could serve as a more effective strategy for advancing AI development. Therefore, it is suggested that the unfalsifiable claim regarding the new AI system should be subject to scrutiny by evaluating whether the proposed system represents an innovative search framework for generating human-level language. If it does, it may mark a notable achievement in applying this framework to a particularly challenging task within the domain of NLP. In contrast, if it does not, it may indicate that the unfalsifiable claim is based on an incorrect understanding of how successful AI systems operate, and this insight could prove valuable for guiding AI research in general. Overall, it is concluded that unfalsifiable claims of reaching human-level performance in complex tasks should be evaluated by analyzing whether the proposed system incorporates an innovative search framework, and this approach holds promise for advancing AI development across a broad range of domains within NLP. ineffective at detecting incidents that are not clearly deviant from normal 
activity, particularly in environments with changing patterns of usage. 
Incident detection would be greatly enhanced by consideration of spatial 
and temporal context in addition to considering the magnitude of deviations 
from typical behavior. Thus, there is a need to develop improved methods 
based on machine learning that can handle data in real-time while also taking 
into account the complex interplay of factors associated with incidents.

unbounded number of categories and classes. In order to address this, an

proposed, incorporating data from social media that can identify incidents

Twitter that was selected at random and also through selection based on 
judgement, showing that it is able to accurately detect incidents when they 
occur, particularly when human judgement is applied to select relevant data.

context from other sources such as maps and calendars to further improve

system for mobile devices is also considered, enabling delivery of detected 
incidents to users as they unfold. The algorithm proposed in this paper is

generalization due to the commonality of the challenges it addresses with

Recent studies have analyzed how deep learning classifiers can be challenged by malicious attacks and proposed methods for verifying the reliability of these classifiers in the face of adversity. Nevertheless, there has been a lack of investigation into utilizing statistical tools to enhance the robustness of deep learning models. This paper introduces an innovative approach that integrates concepts from Bayesian learning and adversarial robustness, resulting in a method called Verifiable Bayesian Adversarial Training (V-BAT). Through this method, we can verify the reliability of deep learning models and, at the same time, prevent overfitting. Experimental findings demonstrate that models created using V-BAT 1) surpass state-of-the-art models in terms of certainty and reliability verification at the test stage, 2) exhibit superior generalization, and 3) show an improvement in performance on both clean and adversarial images. Importantly, the training process of our models is less labor-intensive as it does not require repeatedly generating adversarial examples in the training stage. The benefits of V-BAT can be attributed to the broadening of margins in feature spaces and the incorporation of randomization into models. Moreover, we show that the reliability of deep learning models can be further increased by utilizing data augmentation techniques and higher-capacity models. Interestingly, randomization is found to be the primary factor contributing to the enhancement of reliability. Lastly, we provide a connection between Verifiable BAT and traditional BAT, illustrating that the latter can be viewed as a special case of the former, and highlight potential future research directions in this area. This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of various Spectral Dimensionality Reduction (SDR) techniques in a pixel classification framework, focusing on hyperspectral images. To evaluate the effectiveness of these methods, a comprehensive framework is introduced that assesses four key aspects: computational efficiency, data complexity, feature extraction capabilities, and classification accuracy. Based on the proposed assessment framework, a comprehensive comparison of eight prominent SDR methods is reported, along with a detailed investigation of two top-performing techniques: Linear Spectral Transform (LST) and t-Distributed Scalar Embedding (tSNE). The study reveals that LST offers an optimal balance of computational efficiency and effective feature extraction. Additionally, tSNE is identified as a capable method for complex data sets, albeit suffering from long computation times. Notably, combining LST with other classification methods and data sets yields superior results, underscoring the versatility of LST. Future research directions are also suggested. Furthermore, a publicly accessible Python library containing the proposed framework and experimental results is provided, enabling other researchers to replicate the study and build upon its findings. The study further investigates the potential of LST when integrated with other classification methods, and reveals that combining it with Least Squares Support Vector Machines yields the highest accuracy among 27 tested combinations of SDR methods and classifiers on the considered data sets. The choice of loss function for a deep learning model is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions and classification problems that exist. Current knowledge on loss functions has developed into a somewhat intuitive and heuristic field. In this study, we demonstrate that the optimal loss function for a classification task is often the one with the lowest classification error, a concept we call the 'Optimal Loss Function' (OLF). Our central claim is that the OLF can be reliably identified through a simple, efficient, and universally applicable approach. By defining distinct types of classification problems and examining their characteristics, we provide a framework for understanding and optimizing deep learning models, ultimately leading to better generalization to new datasets and improved performance in the wild. Our empirical analysis, involving over 1,000 evaluations across 7 datasets and 3 scenarios, showcases the effectiveness of our approach and highlights new insights into loss function understanding. Our code and datasets are publicly available for reproduction of our results. One such method being developed involves using a certain class of wavefunctions called Jastrow ansatz to describe the many-body system, and coupled-lattice electron-ion dynamics to simulate the movement of electrons and nuclei. However, when dispatchers are asked to monitor multiple users and incorporate this information into their community safety efforts, they may inadvertently compromise user anonymity. To resolve this issue, we propose an advanced methodology that utilizes a combination of interdisciplinary techniques, including natural language processing, to identify and isolate incident-related details, and thereby enable dispatchers to comply with data protection regulations while effectively performing their jobs. To study the time-dependent nature of musical complexity, we apply the
concept of informational complexity from complexity theory to analysis of
popular Western music spanning across the past millennium. Trajectories of
musical complexity are mapped out, linking late medieval times to the present
day. Our findings show that complexity levels are consistent within a single
era but vastly different across various time periods, enabling the
identification of distinct eras by their corresponding complexity levels. This
study also explores the relationship between complexity and musical scales,
revealing an upward trend in complexity in alignment with scale size. Moreover,
repeated assessments by music experts classify the selected music samples as
representative of five distinct eras - Renaissance, Baroque, Classical, Rom
anti, and Contemporary - all falling under the heading of Western classical
music. This research offers a quantitative measure of musical complexity that
complements existing qualitative assessments. Although based on Western music,
this research lays the groundwork for similar analyses of non-Western styles and
other forms of musical expression.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two main ways: the ATE can be directly estimated from data that includes both treatment and outcome information, known as instrumental variable regression; on the other hand, the ATE can also be estimated by comparing a control group that did not receive the treatment with a group that did receive the treatment, known as difference in means. The key challenge in both methods is addressing the non-random assignment of treatments; this paper focuses on using machine learning models to predict the ATE by analyzing treatment and outcome data, known as the Standardized Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (SAIPW) method. By using SAIPW with a large number of covariates, our simulation studies show that this method has better performance than traditional methods that only use simple probability weighting; this paper also extends the weighting method to handle more complex data structures, known as repeated treatment and outcome data. Furthermore, our study explores the reliability of the ATE estimates under different scenarios of treatment and outcome data missingness. The proposed SAIPW method is compared with other methods that can handle non-random treatment assignment, such as machine learning augmented IPW methods and deep learning based methods that use the ATE's structural equation model. The results of our simulation studies and a real data application on which we tested the ATE estimates' robustness to different patterns of missingness data show that SAIPW outperforms the other methods in terms of mean absolute error. Specifically, SAIPW's performance was enhanced by using a large number of covariates and the weighted loss function was optimized with an additional step that uses the Taylor series approximation, known as Standardized Augmented Inverse Weighted Conditional Expectation (SAIWCe). The advantages of our SAIWCe were seen even in scenarios of limited data; this method has theoretical guarantees on its convergence. The software used in our study, known as standard_ipw, is available at https://github.com/galgar123/standard_ipw. In Offline Reinforcement Learning, pre-trained reinforcement learning agents can be compromised during data collection. We investigate the impact of substitution attacks and introduce the concept of data reliability as a measure to evaluate and mitigate such threats. Specifically, we focus on corruption-resilient RL and establish a theoretical framework to guarantee performance in the presence of data corruption. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm that can adapt to various levels of corruption when collecting data and demonstrate its effectiveness through experimental evaluations. Notably, our approach also maintains optimal off-policy performance in the absence of corruption and surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art RL methods under high levels of corruption. Overall, our research provides a framework for designing robust RL systems capable of withstanding data corruption. We have developed a novel approach for computing these convolutions without resorting to brute force methods, which have a known low-order runtime error. Our method can compute the convolution of two vectors of prime numbers of a fixed number of bits with a runtime of $n^{1+\omega}(n \log n)^{\log 2}$ and two integers of a fixed number of bits with $n^{1+\omega} (n \log n)^{\log 2}$. This represents a nearly linear improvement over the existing brute force solution. Additionally, we have demonstrated that our algorithm can be utilized for computing modular forms and elliptic curve systems with a runtime of $n^{3/2+o(1)}$. Furthermore, we have established an efficient solution for computing the sum of the divisors of a number $n$, which can be achieved in $n^{1+o(1)}$ time. This represents a nearly linear time improvement over the existing solution. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by nonlinearity, non-stationarity, and the presence of anomalies. The dynamic mode decomposition technique has gained significant popularity, allowing for the extraction of system components from high-dimensional data. However, the method's effectiveness is highly dependent on a well-suited kernel function for each system. In many cases, determining an optimal kernel function is a difficult task. This paper introduces LANDO, an advanced kernel optimization method based on sparse regularization, aimed at finding the most suitable kernel function for dynamic mode decomposition. By leveraging sparsity, LANDO reduces the impact of non-essential frequencies and system components, fine-tuning the kernel function to accurately reflect the underlying system dynamics. Through theoretical analysis, the method is proven to outperform or equally effective compared to existing methods. Furthermore, LANDO's utility extends to various applications, including system identification, fault detection, and performance assessment, as demonstrated in the paper's practical examples. Research into the feasibility of regular black hole creation through gravitational collapse has yielded mixed outcomes based on different assumptions regarding the equation of state. A special case, where the equation of state is linear and occurs only when the density is above a certain threshold, has never been explored in the context of isentropic collapse. Our analysis reveals that when this linear equation of state is applied to a mass-distribution derived from the Taylor-Schechter model, massless particles make up an arbitrarily small fraction of the total mass. Consequently, the possibility of forming a regular black hole in this scenario is feasible but highly unlikely. Our findings also highlight that when the equation of state for the Taylor-Schechter model is linear and extends to the ground state density, the resulting collapse behaves similarly to a dust collapse, and regular black hole creation becomes impractical. Ultimately, our research underscores the importance of accurately modeling the equation of state for regular black hole creation, a task that remains complicated due to the lack of observational data in astrophysical environments. Our work also calls into question the validity of recently conducted studies on regular black hole feasibility, particularly those utilizing Taylor-Schechter models with distinct equations of state. Our analysis raises the hope that future research may be able to inform and differentiate from these prior studies. Our work also demands a reevaluation of the notion that spherically symmetric collapse with a linear equation of state necessitates a black hole or no-regular-black-hole outcome. Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the near-extreme black hole horizon mass formula. The Iyer-Wald formalism accurately calculates covariant corrections to the mass/charge relationship. By systematically incorporating higher-order covariant derivatives into our method, we have been able to derive a unified correction term that encompasses a variety of previous approaches. Specifically, our approach subsumes existing results for spin-one and spin-two perturbations, as well as the "most corrected" term in perturbative series. Furthermore, our method's structure allows for a straightforward extension to higher-dimensional scenarios. The application of our method to perturbed Kerr black holes, via an explicit calculation of the axion field, reveals that the resulting correction terms significantly enhance accuracy at masses lower than those associated with the Thorne "correction" mass scale (typically involving thermal black holes). Consequently, we propose that the Iyer-Wald formalism holds promise for systematically improving mass estimates even for supermassive black holes. Moreover, our method may facilitate the development of more precise electromagnetic emission models based on these modified near-horizon geometries. The ultimate goal of this research is to contribute to the resolution of the black hole information paradox through a quantitative analysis of quantum corrections to general relativity, driven by the black hole case study. The plot is symmetric, with the left y-axis representing the integrated correction term and the right y-axis representing the correction terms for the mass/charge relationship.

A common issue with current state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms is that they are unable to generalize effectively to new tasks, even those with minor variations. This study aims to address this challenge by proposing a novel end-effect investigation approach to drive effective motor learning. From a robotic standpoint, the end-effect investigation approach enables a robot to discover a task-dependent coordinate system by analyzing the effects of actions, ultimately allowing for generalization across different tasks. To achieve this, we develop a novel generalization metric, called end-effect investigation, and integrate it with a reinforcement learning algorithm in a novel way. The result is an end-effect investigation-driven reinforcement learning algorithm that facilitates generalization in complex robotic manipulation tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach can effectively transfer skills in a variety of real-world robotic manipulation tasks. We establish a novel framework for gravity and a scalar field by amplifying the vibrant Poincaré algebra, which has a substantial number of commutators, in a four-dimensional spacetime. This work builds upon our previous research, where we generated a novel gauge theory for a massive particle in three-dimensional spacetime with a vibrant Galilean symmetry, a characteristic feature of non-relativistic effects. The developed actions are then generalized to include aspects of non-relativistic gravity. The resulting actions exhibit novel invariance properties, such as Poincaré invariance, a feature not observed in the relativistic Einstein-Hilbert action. Additionally, we derive generalized actions for a massive particle in (3+1) spacetime dimensions. The resulting actions display a rich spectrum of symmetry, both vibrant Galilean and Poincaré, depending on the particle's momentum. This is in sharp contrast to the relativistic particle actions. We also explore the covariant 'folding' procedure to derive the Einstein-Hilbert action from a novel non-relativistic form, a technique reminiscent of double field theory. We further generalize our findings to spacetimes with any number of dimensions. The resulting actions are then applied to a system where the scalar field interacts with a particle, an approach which may be useful in understanding non-relativistic gravity from a quantum field theory perspective. One potential application of this formalism is in modeling liquid flow as a classical limit of bosonic fields. Lastly, we examine the Poisson brackets of our generalized theory and derive the general form of the Einstein equations from this algebraic structure. This approach may provide a useful generalization to the Einstein theory, particularly with the inclusion of rotational terms in non-relativistic gravity. Moreover, we explore the possibility of deriving a generalized 'folding' procedure for double field theory and exceptional field theory in spacetimes with any number of dimensions. This research establishes a novel pathway to derive these theories from a novel 'non-relativistic' form of Einstein-Hilbert theory. One interesting outcome of this formalism is the discovery of a 'double' generalization of the Einstein-Hilbert action, which may have applications in double field theory and exceptional field theory. This research delves into the broader conceptual implications of our findings. This goal is achievable if the graph has a planar subgraph that matches its upward movement constraint. Our study involves exploring methods to expand this subgraph into the entire graph, under upward movement guidance. Specifically, we investigate the complexity of this problem when parameterized by the treewidth of the input graph. Notably, we identify instances of this problem that are solvable in polynomial time when treewidth is considered, whereas the general problem is in NP-complete. Additionally, we find parameterized solutions for a related issue concerning Upward Planarity-Orientation Balance. Specifically, we develop two different algorithms, one with a parameter-dependent runtime and another with a fixed runtime, both of which yield efficient results when the input graph has a bounded treewidth. On the other hand, we prove that many variant problems of our core challenges are solvable in polynomial time when the parameter at question is the number of clusters in graph. Agent recall is essential in visual navigation; previously encountered objects or locations cannot be accessed without memory storage. Currently, existing methods assume unlimited memory capacity and often employ fixed, pre-determined plans or select random options from their memory collection. These approaches fail to consider how agents would manage and utilize available memory space or, alternatively, divide their attention between exploring new information and revisiting previously encountered areas to extract more value. We propose MemoNav, a simple yet effective memory-based navigation method addressing these questions. MemoNav chooses which memories to add to its collection and prioritizes which memories to visit when navigating. We provide comprehensive evidence from multiple datasets, demonstrating MemoNav's superior performance over current methods. Additionally, we offer insights into MemoNav's optimal characteristics through systematic analysis. Our results indicate that MemoNav's supervised version outperforms other methods by significantly reducing navigation time with a more direct path. The supervised version's performance improves as the agent encounters more environments. We also created a web-based dataset featuring real-world locations for further study, referred to as the "Neighborhood Collection." MemoNav's performance with this real-world neighborhood dataset surpasses other methods in both navigation time and direct path ratio. We make MemoNav's code and the Neighborhood Collection publicly available. MemoNav's implementation, along with the Neighborhood Collection, can be accessed at https://github.com/yilb/MemoNav. The Neighborhood Collection can also be accessed at https://www.dropbox.com/s/6j3m8kx7qsvy4qu/NeighborhoodCollection.zip. If you use MemoNav, please cite \{author-year\}. MemoNav's performance is influenced by two key factors: (1) memory insertion and (2) memory visitation. When inserting new memories, MemoNav uses a pre-processed map to identify regions that are difficult to reach and those that provide access to previously under-visited areas. When visiting memories, MemoNav uses two criteria: (a) the proximity of the memory to the current agent position and (b) the degree of under-visitation among the memories collection. MemoNav's under-visitation metric measures the proportion of areas in a memory that have not been covered by the agent's navigation path. MemoNav demonstrates superior performance and offers insights into agent memory management, specifically the trade-off between exploring new information and revisiting previously encountered areas to extract more value. To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells (Femto Cells) by reusing the same licensed spectrum. However, these cells' capabilities were insufficient to support future applications like virtual reality and augmented reality. As a result, operators have sought unlicensed spectrum in the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band, with LAA being the name later assigned by 3GPP. Recent and ongoing LAA deployments, primarily in the US, provide insight into how unlicensed and licensed spectrum interact in practice. This paper summarizes my past, present, and planned research into small cell optimization. Moving forward, I will concentrate on a newly utilized unlicensed band, the 6 GHz frequency, where emerging Wi-Fi and 5G NR technologies are likely to coexist. This unique combination offers a unique opportunity for academia and industry to work together and address the numerous technical challenges and uncertainties surrounding this band's implementation. To address this, we have created a comprehensive and inclusive research agenda, focusing on key issues such as interference, handover, and policy applications. This is being presented as a contribution to the research community. Ongoing and future work will be presented in subsequent papers listed under research projects. The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. To address this issue, a new framework, termed Indecision Forests, is introduced to model argument-based reasoning with quantified uncertainty. Specifically, it leverages existing notions of indecision from modal and epistemic logic to learn under uncertain conditions. This research introduces improved methods for Discarding Pruned Dynamic Time Warping (DPDTW), a previous efficiency enhancement of the pruned DTW (pDTW) distance measure. The original DPDTW strategy was designed to address a significant time complexity issue associated with pDTW, which suffers from an exponential decline with the scale of the query dataset. DPDTW itself has a cubic time complexity, but this can be exacerbated by the presence of a threshold in real-world scenarios, leading to an 'early discard' issue. Our target is to resolve this early discard problem by reducing the threshold effect on the discard criterion, thereby increasing the efficiency of DPDTW. Two novel DPDTW variants are proposed: DPDTW$\beta$ and DPDTW$\gamma$. The former achieves this through the introduction of a new efficiency parameter, $\beta$, which determines the discard criterion based on the minimum local similarity between the first signatory element of the reference sequence and the first elements of the query sequences. The latter, however, uses $\gamma$ to represent the number of elements to be considered for the local similarity assessment. Both DPDTW$\beta$ and DPDTW$\gamma$ are evaluated against existing methods, with our empirical results indicating that they surpass DPDTW in terms of execution speed, while also yielding comparable recall and a comparable number of discards. Consequently, DPDTW$\beta$ and DPDTW$\gamma$ are proven to be best-in-class variants of DPDTW. Two resource-rich application experiments are undertaken to validate our findings: the first employs Python-Bumblebee for the evaluation of DPDTW$\beta$ and DPDTW$\gamma$ in the context of first occurrence of next similar occurrence (FOSNO), while the second uses C++-RapidName for the assessment of these methods in the domain of protein classification. Both experiments are successfully completed, yielding our proposed algorithms to be significantly faster than the current state-of-the-art efficiency optimizing approaches. which measures the accessibility of code segments, yet neglects the quality of 
the testing process and the educator's efforts to guide students. To address 
this gap, we developed TestingTeacher, a novel tool combining inquiry-based 
learning principles with the understanding of educators' inputs, to enhance the 
student learning experience. Through a user study involving 300 students and 
4 instructors, we evaluated the impact of traditional and conceptual feedback 
provided by TestingTeacher on the quality of the testing process and the 
associated educational experience. The results indicate that students using 
TestingTeacher submitted more tests with better code coverage and received 
higher scores than those with other testing tools. Furthermore, instructors 
found TestingTeacher's conceptual feedback and testing suggestions useful in 
facilitating their teaching duties. Building on these findings, we plan to 
continue improving TestingTeacher with features that accommodate various 
teaching styles and learning approaches, thus solidifying its position as a 
comprehensive testing solution for software testing education.

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and finance. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle distinctions or accurately represent the interplay between multiple features. This issue could be addressed by using semantic concept analyses, yet existing methods compromised on either clarity or completeness of the explanation. This paper introduces a novel method that combines concept analysis and Integer Programming to provide definitive, human-readable explanations for each class in DNNs. Our approach evaluates the relevance of each concept to each class, enabling precise control over the inclusion of each concept and resulting in clearer explanations with minimal redundancy. By applying this method to multiple datasets, we demonstrate explanations that surpass the quality of existing alternatives, surpassing the readability of visual methods and the redundancy of rule-based methods. This method is now freely accessible at https://github.com/paulbriais/ExEx. Evaluation results reveal a 35% enhancement in the clarity of explanations and a 95.3% reduction in redundancy over existing explainable AI techniques. This superiority is attributed to the high completeness of our method, as validated by a thorough examination of the results. Our findings indicate that this new approach to explainable AI presents a significant breakthrough in the field. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of diverse materials with unique properties at relatively low temperatures. However, achieving successful distant epitaxy proves challenging due to the competition from other growth mechanisms like pinhole and van der Waals epitaxy. This study explores the epitaxial behavior of the Heusler compound GdPtSb, a compound with a hexagonal structure, on monolayer graphene at temperatures ranging from 400 to 600°C. Experimental results indicate that distant epitaxy occurs at temperatures below 500°C, while higher temperatures result in a combination of distant and pinhole epitaxy. Through the analysis of film surface microscopes and Raman spectroscopy, this work confirms that the epitaxial relationship of the Heusler films grown via distant epitaxy is identified as (123)R3m, with an in-plane rotation of 30 degrees. This study demonstrates that the equilibrium between different growth mechanisms can be influenced by temperature and possibly other factors, such as substrate-film adhesion and the presence of a substrate-film interface. This work also suggests an alternative definition for remote epitaxy, requiring not only a substrate rotation but also the absence of direct epitaxial contact between the substrate and film. This redefinition enables the classification of many films as having a remote epitaxial relationship. This study provides crucial insights into the epixyl mechanism, contributing to the development of a more general theory involving a multi-atom epitaxy process. Additionally, this work explores the possibility of using Heusler compounds, known for their unique properties and magnetic characteristics, in spintronics and other devices. This study opens up new avenues for the spintronic and optoelectronic applications of Heusler films and paves the way for the synthesis of other materials with exotic properties using the remote epitaxy technique. In conclusion, this study delves into the monodomain growth of Heusler films via distant epitaxy, obtaining nearly single-domain Heusler films with a 30-degree in-plane rotation and providing new perspectives on remote epitaxy and van der Waals epitaxy. This work confirms that temperature plays a crucial role in the epitaxial relationship between films and substrates, leading to a deeper comprehension of the Heusler film growth process. Recent JWST observations of El Gordo, the massive galaxy cluster, have identified 23 known groups of multiply distorted galaxy images and 8 previously undiscovered ones, all verified spectroscopically by MUSE. By analyzing these groups, researchers created a lens model which allowed them to locate 37 more groups, comprising 23 new and 14 previously identified ones. Based on the initial lens model, researchers estimated the positions of 87 observed galaxy images, 83 of which were subsequently verified by MUSE. Spectroscopic data revealed 37 new and unidentified galaxy images, out of a total of 121. Furthermore, the calculations point to the presence of a massive, distant, and previously unknown source, later confirmed by MUSE as a red supergiant star at a staggering 6.2 Gpc distance. This discovery not only sets a new record for the farthest known star but also makes El Gordo the third galaxy cluster found to act as a gravitational lens in the past few years. Further analysis using the galaxy cluster's model predicted an unprecedented level of magnification for its center, with estimates as high as 26. Additionally, the study identifies a previously unseen state of a galaxy, specifically ALESS 041.1, which exhibits extremely high levels of magnification and distortion without being identified as the source of multiple image systems. The discovery of this system, along with various other notable observations, showcases the remarkable capabilities of the JWST in its observation of the massive galaxy cluster, ACT-CL J0102$-$4915, also known as "El Gordo". The study verifies 29 of 30 proposed multiple image systems and uncovers 18 newly identified systems, further highlighting the extensive and unparalleled views of the galaxy cluster provided by the JWST. This approach allows us to extend the GNS construction itself to a functor, where the mapping is consistent across various categories of algebras and their representations. This new mathematical representation, the 2-functor, is capable of addressing issues related to the solvability of the inverse GNS construction. Furthermore, our research includes a similar analysis of the covariant version of the GNS construction, which is relevant to situations where the mapping from states to their corresponding algebras is not universal. This leads to a broader mathematical framework, the 2-category of covariant GNS constructions. Additionally, our research demonstrates that both the GNS and its covariant version 2-functors form a certain type of structured mathematical objects known as strict fricatally-annotated 2-functors. The field of cosmology has experienced significant breakthroughs, thanks in large part to the introduction of inflationary theories. Among these, models exhibiting $\alpha$-attractor behavior hold significant promise. Not only do they display an appealing simplicity, but their properties also remain largely unchanged for varying values of their key parameter, with exceptions being cases with vanishing $\alpha$. In this article, we delve into the realm of $\alpha$-attractor models, showcasing their various forms such as models with fractional powers and multiple stages. We also examine their underlying properties and how these models are distinguished within the framework of the Starobinsky model. Furthermore, we discuss predictions derived from observational data as well as implications arising from constraints imposed by the Planck dataset, with implications for the field of cosmology. Additionally, we explore Dirac-Born-Infeld $\alpha$-attractor models, highlighting their K-essence properties and embeddability within the Veneziano mechanism. With respect to these DBI models, we explore the stability of their solutions in an expanded framework, with consideration for the impact of non-minimal coupling on their stability. In conclusion, we review the assess the feasibility of these models in the context of current and future observational experiments. With respect to future experiments such as the Square Kilometre Array, we find that these models may enable the determination of the Hubble constant with remarkable precision, to the order of $0.3\%$, in conjunction with other findings such as the amplitude of density fluctuations and the tensor-to-scalar ratio. In addition, we explore the scope of model predictions with respect to the phase transition in the density perturbation spectrum, identifying potential future discoveries with the help of forthcoming observational data such as the Future Surveyc. With these considerations in mind, we examine the feasibility of model testing and validation in the era of galaxy-scale surveys, including the DESI project, and future linear matter spectrum low-$k$ analysis, and nonlinear matter spectrum analysis with future surveys such as the Future Surveyc. In this article, we explore potential future discoveries such as the determination of the Hubble constant from the phase space of matter distribution, and the potential future discovery of non-Gaussianity in the galaxy distribution, in addition to the already identified potential future discoveries with the Future Surveyc. This study initiates a cross-country analysis of the distribution of portfolio returns, 
which is essential for capital allocation and performance evaluation in financial management. 
A normal-based analysis is presented, along with an alternative method that 
does not require data to follow a normal distribution. 
The applications of portfolio return analysis are then examined in detail. 
Notably, this research diverges from a related study that focused on portfolio risk 
by utilizing the mean absolute return rather than the mean return. 
Additionally, it addresses a void in literature regarding the estimation of benchmark 
beta using an average absolute deviation measure and modifies the CAPM to account for 
non-normal data distributions. 
Finally, this study explores how portfolio return distributions change 
over time in different countries and proposes a method for identifying the most 
advantageous investment opportunities. 
Key findings reveal that the distribution of portfolio returns varies significantly 
from a normal distribution in various countries and that the most profitable 
investment opportunities can be found by analyzing the most extreme returns. 
Furthermore, this study reveals that the most advantageous investment opportunities 
can also be found by comparing the performance of individual stocks. 
Ultimately, this study highlights the practical significance of analyzing 
portfolio return distributions in different countries. 
Key findings are presented through tables and graphs for countries with 
longest available data series and the highest market capitalization. 
Notably, this study analyzes data from the United States, Japan, the UK, Germany, 
France, Australia, and Canada. 
A set of methods for replicating the results and the associated R code are available online. 
This study also complements existing research on the analysis of 
portfolio return distributions and provides a new perspective on capital 
allocation and performance evaluation in financial management. 
In particular, this research can be seen as a response to existing studies 
by Fama and Kendall (1959), Black and Scholes (1973), Sharpe (1963), 
Black and Scholes (1973), and Jensen (1968).

investment firms, and their clients, as well as financial professionals, 
managers, and analysts.

the most advantageous investment opportunities and provides answers 
to practical questions from these groups.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care technology called cardiac auscultation has the potential to improve this.  However, accurate identification of cardiac sounds is hindered by background noise and the practitioner's skill level.  To address this challenge, a new method involving a neural network inspired by the structure of the human auditory system has been developed.  By incorporating a feature extraction layer that mimics the characteristics of the human ear and a classifier capable of learning from its own inputs, this neural network is capable of learning in a data-driven manner.  Additionally, the effectiveness of this model was tested under conditions of artificial and real noise as well as altered sound quality, and it performed significantly better than existing methods.  Validation was conducted using a standard dataset, and the model was also tested using a novel cardiac auscultation dataset specifically designed to simulate varying levels of noise and signal distortion.  As a result, this model demonstrated a significant improvement in classification performance compared to existing methods.  Code and model information are available for public access. Our research examined how online communities respond to shared challenges, focusing on climate change. Specifically, we investigated the impact of a collective goal on the behavior of users within a climate-related online forum. The study revealed that goal-oriented messaging can boost user contributions, but only if users feel a sense of community and accountability. Interacting with others in a online space does not necessarily yield cooperative behavior; it is essential to foster a sense of community to leverage the potential of social interactions for achieving collective goals. The full details of this study can be found in the linked paper. Based on these findings, developers of online platforms can employ strategies to enhance user cooperation and cooperation-led innovation, particularly in domains like climate change by promoting a sense of community among users. This study offers an empirical examination of the concept of trustworthiness in auctions, specifically in a second-price auction setting with both patient and impulsive agents. We introduce the idea of trustworthiness as a key factor determining a seller's willingness to establish a long-term relationship with a buyer. A buyer's level of trustworthiness is measured by their probability of winning auctions, whereas a seller's level of trustworthiness is measured by their probability of engaging in a long-term relationship with a buyer. We found that both patient and impulsive agents place a high value on trustworthiness, with the latter valuing it the highest. Furthermore, we discovered that a positive history of past auctions significantly increases a seller's level of trustworthiness, particularly among impulsive agents. Conversely, a negative history reduces a seller's level of trustworthiness, with a greater decline observed among patient agents. Our results also reveal that a significant disparity exists in the level of trustworthiness between impulsive and patient agents, with the latter being significantly higher. Lastly, we observed that a seller's level of trustworthiness is directly correlated with their revenue in a series of long-term auction sequences. Our findings imply that a long-term, patient-based approach to business relationships is founded on a strong foundation of trustworthiness. Additionally, we can adapt the concept of trustworthiness to any repeated game or interaction. Finally, we propose several theoretical and practical aspects of our study that warrant further exploration.

ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. The advancement in computational capabilities and machine learning methods has enabled researchers to investigate the use of resting-state fMRI imaging data for classifying ADHD. Unlike previous studies that focused on the entire brain, this study's aim is to identify the essential brain regions for improving ADHD diagnosis. By employing a novel two-stage classification model, the study evaluated 13 essential brain regions while selecting the most critical components, ultimately revealing the diagnostic value of the default mode network for ADHD. Specifically, the results showed that the posterior cerebellum was found to be significantly active during ADHD-related tasks and exhibited a 33% improvement in accuracy after component selection. This improvement demonstrated that selecting the most relevant brain regions can elevate ADHD diagnosis accuracy from 88.7% to 91.4%. The study's findings will facilitate the development of more efficient and accurate machine learning algorithms for ADHD diagnosis by focusing on key brain regions. Moreover, the study's observations contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying neurobiological mechanisms of ADHD. Ultimately, the study's outcomes will lead to the development of more effective diagnostic tools for ADHD, such as fMRI data for clinical use. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. To address this, MadDog is an web-based system designed for acronym detection and disambiguation purposes. Combining both machine learning and rule-based techniques, MadDog leverages a multi-dimensional approach that incorporates domain information to enhance accuracy. The system offers a user-friendly interface for users to input documents or paste text, allowing them to access the system via a web interface or integrate it into their existing applications using APIs. MadDog is currently available at http://madgud.i3s.unibe.ch. Experimental evaluations validate MadDog's competitiveness with leading commercial systems, showcasing its ability to accurately identify and define acronyms in standard, domain-specific, and diverse texts. Notably, MadDog demonstrates exceptional performance on legal texts, outperforming other systems by a significant margin. Evaluations confirm that the system's efficient and scalable processing capabilities allow it to achieve high speeds, making it suitable for large-scale data processing. Last but not least, MadDog's flexible design enables it to be integrated into various applications, as demonstrated by two use-case studies involving the system's deployment in a university law library and a comparative legal research project. Overall, MadDog is a substantial addition to the field of acronym processing, offering a range of features that set it apart from other available systems. We introduce novel, sublinear quantum algorithms for estimating the unbiased von Neumann entropy of a quantum state $\rho$. The first algorithm employs a random quantum circuit $U$ followed by measuring its output state to obtain an $O(\epsilon^{-1}\lambda^{-2})$ error estimate using $O(\epsilon^{-1}\lambda^{-4})$ quantum computations, where $\lambda$ represents the spectral gap of $\rho$.
