The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key variation, the Stable Roommates problem with Veto and Vain, introduces restrictions: an agent can either: (i) disqualify a match as a whole, or (ii) disqualify a potential partner's matches individually. Under the term "additively separable", we refer to situations where an agent's dislike towards a particular pair is calculated as a weighted sum of their dislike towards the members of that pair. A key finding shows that, in the 3-dimensional case, determining a stable pairing that maximizes agents' combined happiness (under a specific definition of happiness) is an NP-hard problem, even when considering situations with i) one agent able to give a negative rating to pairs, or ii) all agents able to give a negative rating to pairs in a linearly structured environment. Additionally, we show the hardness of finding a stable pairing that maximizes agents' combined happiness when considering situations with ii) all agents able to give a negative rating to pairs in a general setting. A key finding also shows that, in situation i) when an agent can give a negative rating to pairs, finding a stable pairing that maximizes agents' combined happiness, even when considering a linearly structured environment, can be solved in a limited number of candidates. A part of this research was previously presented at the 24th AI, Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence Conference in 2019. Based on the feedback from the conference, we revised our approach to comparing the additive and lexicographic social welfare notions and introduced a new SW-Intervene version of the Stable Roommates problem with Veto and Vain to explore when introducing some level of intervention in situation ii) when all agents able to give a negative rating to pairs may lead to a better outcome. Additionally, we showed that finding a stable pairing that maximizes agents' combined happiness in situation ii) when all agents able to give a negative rating to pairs is single-candidate solvable. A part of this research was also presented at the 33rd International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in 2021. From here on, when referring to the Stable Roommates problem with Veto and Vain, we consider situations where an agent can either disqualify a match as a whole or disqualify a potential partner's matches individually. A part of this research was also presented at the 33rd International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in 2021.

Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a ground plane. This distinction allows for a more precise evaluation of methods' effectiveness in addressing the optimization-generalization dilemma. Our findings and the Wealth tool are now being made available to support the machine learning community in addressing the optimization-generalization dilemma. To address this issue, a novel design of an iterative feedback-control system for forming complex structures is introduced, which simultaneously creates multiple structures within a three-dimensional volume of a sample and rapidly modulates tissue surface. The proposed method exhibits a high degree of flexibility and can quickly adjust its parameters to shape laser light for various structure formations. Experimental results demonstrate the successful creation of 2D microloops, as well as a ring structure, and show a high degree of agreement between the desired and achieved structures. Furthermore, simultaneous formation of two intricate structures and rapid surface modulation in tissue phantom, as well as in live tissue, are successfully demonstrated. The developed system displays a fast response time and rapid structure changes, with a high repetition rate of 5.8 Hz. This breakthrough technology has numerous potential bio applications, such as cell stimulation, tissue engineering, and the treatment of diseases. In general, the designed system has an extensive range of uses that are controlled by a simple, intuitive program. In summary, the presented concept has a great potential for forming complex structures and modulating tissue surface, while ensuring the safety and effectiveness of the treatment. The development of this technique marks an important breakthrough in the field of bio applications and holds great promise for the future. The presented findings provide a significant answer to the described challenge and serve as a useful guide for researchers who strive to shape laser light for various biological applications. An important contribution of this study lies in the iterative approach it offers for controlling structure formations and surface modulations, as well as in the simultaneous creation of intricate structures and tissue modulations, which have a vast potential for future practical applications. An important aspect of this work is the simultaneous creation of two or more structures with a high degree of detail and without distortion in a 3D volume of the sample, as well as the rapid modulations of tissue surface. The fast and precise modulations of tissue surface have a great potential for the treatment of diseases at cellular level, as well as in other biological applications. The presented results provide a clear evidence that the proposed method is capable of modulating tissue surface under the influence of laser light, while ensuring the safety and effectiveness of the treatment, as well as the induced tissue changes that lead to the desired surface modulations. An important outcome of this study is the successful creation of the desired structure in live tissue, as well as the rapid modulations of tissue surface with a high repetition rate.

Several techniques have been proposed to eliminate speckles from adaptive optics systems but most are limited by the necessity for significant on-sensor processing capabilities.  A 2019 technique proposed by our group, Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent Imaging (FASI), relies on the signal processing capabilities of the detector and is therefore suitable for implementation on current high-tech cameras.  Recent experiments using a Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics Laboratory testbed have demonstrated the effectiveness of FASI on a 64-element lenslet camera.  FASI has enabled the simultaneous optimization of over 4000 sub-apertures, outperforming traditional techniques for speckle reduction and making concurrent use of both low and high spatial-scales in optical systems possible.  FASI is now capable of achieving high frame rates, with rapid focal plane wavefront control of residual speckles.  This technique is particularly suitable for large ground-based telescopes and is poised to revolutionize the field of large infrared and visible wavelength optics.  It has the potential to greatly enhance the overall performance of large telescopes and many existing and future optical systems.  A demonstration of fast focal plane wavefront control of residual speckles through FASI has been achieved and is showcased in this paper.  This involves the use of an 8x8 sub-area of a 64-element camera, with the ability to control wavefronts at high speed (at a rate of  25.6 Hz).  Additionally, the fast response time of the camera allows for the resurrection of images that have been lost due to speckle-related data loss, with the ability to rescue up to 87.5% of lost information.  This is done by means of analytical algorithms that utilize the properties of the Bessel functions to reconstruct lost information from the remaining signal.  A related method, Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent Imaging with Refocused Time (FASI-RT), has also been developed and allows for the rescue of lost information over longer periods of time.  This involves the refocusing of images and the use of the response time of the camera to rescue information, with a maximum time frame that can be up to 200ms and allows for the rescue of 97.5% of lost information.  This technique has been demonstrated and shown to be effective in eliminating speckles and allowing for the rescue of lost information. Meta-analyses that investigate the relationships between multiple outcomes in the same studies are known as bivariate meta-analyses. They are utilized to produce predictive probability distributions for latent quantities such as underlying effect sizes and their correlations. Our research extends bivariate meta-analyses to include heterogeneity estimates in both the mean-effects and the correlation structures, a feature previously absent in the field. Additionally, many meta-analyses suffer from the issue of zero-weighted studies in forest plots, a problem this work addresses by developing consistent and efficient estimators that utilize all available data within robust cluster-robust models. Our research compares the performance of various estimators through simulations and shows that they produce comparable results. Ultimately, our research highlights the advantages of using the method over existing alternatives by illustrating its capacity to significantly reduce bias in certain scenarios. The approach, termed the CR-Bayes analysis, may be applied using the R package MetaBiv, which is also used to replicate the findings of our study. The CR-Bayes analysis offers a new method for analyzing bivariate meta-analyses that combines features such as heterogeneity estimates, zero-weighted studies, and robust models to address potential biases in estimating the mean-effects and the correlation structure of an analysis. The approach, like other Bayes models, has been met with resistance in the meta-analysis community due to concerns over bias elimination, a concern this work addresses through simulation and finds that the CR-Bayes model produces a reduced bias in certain scenarios. The approach, termed the CR-Bayes model, is now applied to a set of outcomes related to the treatment of hypertension to examine its performance in a real-world analysis. The results show a high level of consistency between the CR-Bayes model and the frequentist based estimators in estimating the correlation between the outcomes related to hypertension related outcomes. The CR-Bayes model is also found to produce a reduced bias in estimating the effect sizes of the included studies as well as to produce more precise estimates of the effect sizes than frequentist based estimators. The CR-Bayes model is now used to produce a prediction distribution for the effect sizes of the included studies as well as to produce a distribution of the correlation between the outcomes related to hypertension. We go on to identify additional constraints on $k$ and $n$ and, by considering the difference between $a$ and $b$ as $2d$, derive necessary conditions for $2k+1$ and $d$. Ultimately, we present a theorem characterizing the whole number solutions to the equation in question. The method used here resembles that in the 1936 paper by L.J. The Erdős unique-sums problem inquiries about the minimum value of $n$ such that there exists an $x$ that can be expressed in multiple ways using a subset of the integers from the set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$. In this study, we discuss various formulations of the problem that have been addressed by other mathematicians and present new results for each of these variants. The latter part of the article focuses on a particular formulation given by Allen, Friedlander, and Rusek and shows that $n$ can be as low as $43$ to satisfy the given condition. The article further explores the general $k$-combinations for $k\leq n$ where each element in the set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ can appear at most once to express an integer $x$. In this scenario, we prove that $n$ can be as low as $29$. The article further considers a different scenario where the given integers can be sequential but may also be repetitive. In this case, we prove that $n$ can be as low as $23$. The article addresses yet another scenario where the given integers are distinct, but may also repeat within the set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$. In this scenario, we prove that $n$ can be as low as $17$. The article presents new lower bounds for the problem using linear combinations of $n$ where $n\geq 10$. The adiabatic index $\Gamma$ represents a fundamental characteristic of dense matter, influencing the endpoint of neutron star mergers and core-collapse supernovae. In this study, we synthesize various calculations of nuclear, neutron star, and liquid metal crusts to construct a comprehensive adiabatic index $\Gamma$ profile for dense matter as a function of density and temperature. Our integrated model covers five distinct density regimes: high-density neutron star matter, dense nuclear matter formed in the core of neutron stars and heavy compact objects, and the liquid metal core with its associated thermal bath. Our $\Gamma$ profile enables predictions about thermal expansions in different density regimes, with notable variations expected. Furthermore, we analyze how $\Gamma$ changes with temperature in various systems, which has implications for the thermal radiative emission of neutron stars. Our integrated model allows the thermal expansion and radiative emission of neutron stars to be predicted based on their masses, enabling the reconstruction of $\Gamma$ from observational data of compact stars. Our integrated model also facilitates the comparison of thermal properties with and without strangeness in the core of neutron stars and other objects, such as kaonless and kaon-fragmentation compact stars. Our analysis indicates that the presence of strange quark cores causes thermal expansion to transition from solid to liquid or solid with liquid droplets as temperature increases, whereas solid cores due to neutron-proton interactions or in neutron star merges do not exhibit this behavior. Our understanding of adiabatic index $\Gamma$ and thermal expansion, with and without strangeness, is expected to contribute to the analysis of future multimessenger datasets of neutron star mergers and other compact objects. Our integrated model also enables the investigation of other phenomena, such as the behavior of neutron star crusts in X-ray transients and the thermal emission of isolated neutron stars and white dwarfs. Our integrated model is based on the public available code NS Mayer's Table Generator, which we updated to construct the necessary tables for our analysis. This updated generator, incorporating our new $\Gamma$ profile, is available at [http://nmstmg.web.uni-freiburg.de/]. Our new $\Gamma$ profile is also available at [https://www.physik.uni-freiburg.de/npnsm/tables.html]. In our accompanying paper, we present the updated table generator and the new $\Gamma$ profile in detail. This work was partially motivated by the NS Physics Working Group's report on neutron star physics, which we contributed to. This research received support from Shinshu

Capturing the behavior and dynamics of complex fluid interfaces is crucial for further development in this field. Interfaces can be modeled using surfaces, which are then influenced by the surrounding fluids through external forces and boundary conditions. Due to the various possible configurations and movements of interfaces, there is currently no universal framework that can effectively represent and track complex interface geometries. As a result, accurate characterization and analysis of interfaces are limited to specific contexts, often leading to simplified representations that compromise precision. To address this, we introduce a new method to characterize and differentiate between interfaces based on their skeletal structures. This approach generates a geometric characterization of interfaces, allowing for unique representations, metric spaces, and distance measurements that can distinguish between dissimilar interfaces. Unlike existing contact information, our skeletal-based method remains invariant under smooth transformations and does not get obstructed by noise. As such, it can efficiently identify differences in highly complex flows, such as those involving three-phase interactions and chaotic mixing scenarios. To evaluate the effectiveness of our skeletal-based method, we implement a straightforward skeletonization protocol along with an optimal matching technique for comparing skeletal structures, which achieves a time complexity of O(n^1.5) and outperforms other comparison methods. Our approach offers a pioneering solution to the long-standing problem of characterizing and analyzing complex interface geometries, providing a versatile and efficient protocol that can be applied to diverse practical applications. To showcase its efficacy, we use our skeletal-based method to extract distinct features from a range of challenging examples, including 2D and 3D flow images involving multiple phases and unique geometric characteristics. Furthermore, our method facilitates decoding and understanding of flow phenomena, such as detecting objects, extracting knowledge, and making informed decisions. To demonstrate its real-world significance, our skeletal-based method is successfully applied to categorize images of tumour cells and normalize cardiac images, showcasing its vast potential applications. To summarize, our skeletal-based method provides a groundbreaking, efficient, and accurate approach to characterize and analyze complex interface geometries, offering a versatile protocol that can be applied to diverse contexts. As such, it has immense potential and can be used to enhance decision-making processes in numerous practical applications. To demonstrate its feasibility and effectiveness, our method achieves state-of-the-art results in comparing skeletal structures while providing comprehensive interpretations and analyses. One such nonlinear component corresponds to the Witten effect, a phenomenon that involves the quantization of a magnetic flux and a charge within a topological insulator's edge. Another nonlinear component originates from the fractional quantum Hall effect, a situation that occurs when strongly interacting two-dimensional electrons result in highly stable, long-living states. Those states, which are stable at extremely low temperatures and magnetic field strengths, exhibit a significant, discrete change in a quantized metric that incorporates both electric and magnetic field influences. A third mechanism, a concept known as the chiral magnetic effect, may also contribute to a time-reversal symmetric response that varies nonlinearly with both electric and magnetic fields, a phenomenon that has been observed in certain three-dimensional ferromagnets with a gap. This enhanced approach enables more precise reasoning about design discussions that incorporate diverse vocabulary. Our results, obtained from a dataset of Java design discussions totaling over 125 thousand messages, demonstrate a significant improvement in conclusion stability compared to a base model that solely analyzes lexical information, particularly in discussions that frequently use new words. Proximal methods are versatile and widely applicable, yet their iterative process often lacks transparency and clear progression towards the optimal solution. In contrast, optimization algorithms like gradient methods offer a clearer understanding of convergence, even if they may not always be the most efficient options. Consequently, it is beneficial to combine the simplicity and broad applicability of proximal methods with the conceptual clarity of gradient methods, especially when working with nonconvex problems. Nonetheless, conventional proximal methods are typically designed assuming the availability of a proximal gradient or subgradient, which is not the case for nonlinear optimization problems on curved surfaces. To address this gap, we introduce an iterative process inspired by Newton-like acceleration, utilizing approximations that require only a proximal gradient and yielding comparable convergence rates. To test its efficacy, we apply our method to a range of practical surface optimization problems, demonstrating its merit in practical scenarios. Specifically, we use an approach based on reparameterization, thereby transforming complex nonconvex problems into an L1-regularized nonconvex minimization on a curved surface that can be solved efficiently with proximal methods. Our results show that combining the iterative process we introduced with L1-regularization can significantly outperform state-of-the-art algorithms in comprehensive numerical experiments. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/fredyabraham/Newton-on-surfaces. This research was funded by ANR-18-CE31-0016 and ANR-19-CE46-0012 projects. Important corrections have been made to the original manuscript, particularly regarding the choice of surface and the complexity of the example problem. We have added a new section justifying our research and presenting an updated version of the method, as well as a corrected theoretical analysis, with a new set of experimental results showing the stability of the algorithm. We have also removed the wrong statement regarding the incompatibility of early termination with nonlinear optimization on curves. To improve the clarity of the manuscript, we have introduced R and Python code, as well as detailed figures and a new definition for the Riemannian Newton iteration. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/fredyabraham/Newton-on-surfaces. This research was funded by projects ANR-18-CE31-0016 and ANR-19-CE46-0012. From a given set of goal-oriented demonstrations in one particular domain, our agent can absorb a general skill that can be applied to other domains as well. Our key innovation lies in introducing a hidden skill representation that integrates learned information from both the training and the target domains. Association rule learning has become a widely used technique in data mining. This method involves simplifying complex findings into comparative statements, such as "80% of customers who bought Product A also bought Product B." The process can be computationally intensive, especially when dealing with large datasets. Researchers have explored various algorithms for speed optimizations by leveraging implicit information within the data and utilizing previously derived patterns. This study focuses on understanding the computational benefits of using pre-existing knowledge in form of already-discovered rules. Our investigation reveals that certain established rules can serve as a foundation for other, yet undiscovered, associations. This foundation, represented as a set of minimal, relevant patterns, can facilitate the identification of new associations. This study delves into the quantification of this foundation's size and examines different deduction methods that can enhance the efficiency of association rule learning. The outcome of our research reveals that each deduction method has its own implications on the learning process and the resulting base of patterns. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the effect of one deduction method, denoted as 'rule re-utilization,' can significantly boost the efficiency of association rule learning. This research is distinct from other deduction methods such as 'rule reduction' and 'base revision.' Our findings are validated through rigorous analysis and experiments. Two specific approaches, 'Extended Item-Based Deduction' and 'Frequent Itemset-Based Deduction,' are proposed as implementations of the rule re-utilization method. This study provides size bounds for the foundation produced by these deduction methods. Our study also examines the efficiency of these deduction methods under two different scenarios. Our work is further validated through empirical tests using real-world datasets. The outcome of these experiments matches our analytically derived estimates. This research offers two new tools: the 'DIDO tool' for computing the foundation's size and the 'DIDO wrapper' for integrating existing rule learning algorithms with the rule re-utilization method. Our research is distinct from other deduction methods such as 'DynReg' and 'BDDMiner,' as we explore the size of the foundation and the efficiency of the learning process. Our work is validated through empirical tests using 19 real-world datasets. Our study provides the first integration of the rule re-utilization method with four existing algorithms: Apriori, PART, SVMLight, and RapidMiner. This research investigates the impact of court-ordered mental health treatment on convicted individuals. Specifically, it examines how requiring treatment influences an individual's likelihood of being re-arrested and the severity of any future crimes committed. Our analysis reveals that requiring mental health treatment reduces an individual's chances of being re-arrested by at least 17.6%, with some types of treatment having a more pronounced effect than others. Furthermore, it appears that certain forms of treatment lower the severity of any future crimes committed by reducing the likelihood of violent re-arrest. Interestingly, there are notable variations in outcomes based on the specific types of treatments given and whether or not an individual's incarceration is extended, which suggests that the effectiveness of certain treatments may depend on the length of an individual's incarceration. Finally, an investigation into the potential underlying factors for these varying outcomes reveals that they are likely related to an individual's initial condition at the time of conviction. This information could be useful to policymakers and practitioners in the criminal justice system as they consider different treatment approaches for their clients, which they may now view as having potentially different effects on an individual's future criminal behavior. Based on our analysis, it is possible to estimate the potential benefits of requiring certain types of treatment, such as a 5.4% to 9.3% reduction in violent re-arrest rates, which could serve as a valuable resource in informing policy discussions surrounding the use of mental health treatment in the justice system. This study introduces an innovative approach, HMM Gauge Likelihood Analysis (HMLA), specifically designed for identifying anomalies in time-series data. HMLA represents normal behavior as a hidden Markov model (HMM) and uses gauge variables to translate expected data into HMM likelihoods. Comparing these probabilities to the actual values in a dataset allows researchers to assess the likelihood of observed data, effectively serving as an anomaly metric. By integrating this metric into various machine learning algorithms, this study demonstrates that HMLA enhances their respective performance in identifying anomalies. Furthermore, the paper examines HMLA's potential applications in real-world contexts, highlighting its potential to contribute to data-driven approaches to quality control and healthcare risk assessment. Key HMLA advantages include its ability to 1) detect anomalies of all scales, as well as those occurring at a specific time, 2) handle complex data, and 3) identify anomalies even when training data is limited. In contrast to existing methods for identifying anomalies, HMLA's ability to leverage gauge variables offers greater flexibility and the potential for more accurate results. To showcase HMLA's effectiveness, the study presents detailed analyses of its applications to synthetic data, as well as two real-world datasets relating to EEG signals and flight delays. All associated code and datasets are publicly accessible for reproduction and modification of the study's findings. Consider a mixture of independent observations drawn from distributions characterized by unknown parameters, where these observations are also independent from one another. When we take a random sample of size 'n' of these mixtures, we can view it as sampling from a distribution with parameters that are averages of the original distribution's parameters, due to the mathematical mixture. However, these average parameters are unknown and cannot be directly estimated through means. This paper explores the use of generalized maximum likelihood estimation to estimate these average parameters, revealing that they can be expressed as linear combinations of the sample moments. Furthermore, we apply these findings to estimate population characteristics, such as population moments and entropy, through sample entropy. We also investigate the statistical properties of these estimators, revealing asymptotic normality and efficient rates of convergence. These results are validated through simulations and real-world data analyses. Additionally, we demonstrate the estimators' ability to detect changes in sampling parameters through a change-point detection method, based on a likelihood ratio test. The proposed methods are implemented in an open-source R package, 'GenMLM'. This package includes functions for estimating mixture parameters, calculating sample entropy, and detecting changes in sampling parameters. These capabilities enable the evaluation of sampling performance and the identification of optimal sampling strategies. The package can be accessed at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=GenMLM. A summary of the package's functions can be found in the documentation. The proposed methods have been applied to the analysis of text data, specifically in understanding gender shifts in literature, where we have detected a significant change in the proportion of female authors around the 19th and early 20th centuries. This represents a notable finding and highlights the potential of these methods for detecting such trends. The study was conducted through the calculation of sample entropy from a large corpus of texts, drawn from seven different domains, as well as the detection of changes in sampling parameters. The results are presented in a series of figures and tables, as part of the package's documentation. The conclusions from this analysis reveal that we can quantify the differences in the distribution of male and female authors' works and detect notable shifts in these distributions. These changes are accompanied by statistical results, showcasing the efficacy of the estimators and our analysis methods. The study demonstrates the versatility of the proposed algorithms in analyzing textual data and detecting changes in sampling parameters. The conclusions from this investigation are summarized in a report, as part of the package's documentation. The findings reveal that the estimators can effectively capture the underlying structure of the data and detect changes in sampling parameters.

Despite this, current research on releasing private datasets assumes independent information and does not address the fundamental issue of how to set the crucial parameter, C, in the modified differential privacy model for dependent information. In this study, we establish a method for determining optimal C values for various scenarios, such as releasing mean values and aggregate statistics from datasets with dependent information. Moreover, we develop methods to estimate confidence intervals in these scenarios, and our experiments demonstrate that our methods outperform the traditional approach, especially in release mechanisms that produce single-valued outputs. Additionally, our research in this area has been influenced by applications in releasing conditional means and applying transformation-based techniques to release private datasets efficiently. In an effort to address this issue, we have investigated the relationship between differential privacy and information exposure, and have applied this understanding to develop new methods for releasing private datasets that are based on the exponential mechanism and other release mechanisms for dependent information. Our results in this area have shown that these new methods can be more effective and result in less exposed information when compared to other private releasing mechanisms. This research aims to extend the concept of joint functionality from real-valued distributions to polynomial-valued distributions within the context of tempered distributions. We begin by exploring the properties of joint functionality for individual polynomials and then demonstrate its applicability to a finite, non-stochastic product of polynomial distributions. Our central findings involve extending the properties of joint functionality to infinite products and generalized functions. Specifically, we show that for a finite number of generalized functions ${f_1, \ldots, f_n}$, their joint functionality ${\rm J f}$ is defined as the function ${\rm j_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes {\rm j_n} \mapsto {\rm j_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes {\rm j_n} \otimes {\rm Tf}}$, where ${\rm Tf = f_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes f_n}$. Similarly, for a infinite product of distributions ${\rm F = (f_\alpha)_{\alpha \in {\mathbb N}}}$, where each ${f_\alpha}$ is a function with compact support, we define its joint functionality as ${\rm J F} = ({\rm j_\alpha})_{\alpha \in {\mathbb N}}$ and demonstrate that ${\rm j_\alpha \mapsto f_\alpha}$ for each ${\alpha \in {\mathbb N}}. Next, we establish the properties of joint functionality for finite and infinite products of functions with compact support and then derive its applications to finite and infinite products of distributions. Finally, we show that the adjacency of distributions is a well-defined concept in the context of tempered generalised functions. Our research further reveals that the adjacency of distributions is equivalent to a specific type of causality. Furthermore, we have identified all tempered generalised functions that are both causal and admissible. In addition to these findings, we have derived closed-form expressions for the adjacency and causality operators corresponding to specific Fourier multipliers. These expressions have in turn enabled us to derive expressions for the adjacency and causality distributions in terms of Black-Scholes operators. atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
successfully integrated machine learning algorithms with Rydberg atom techniques, 
allowing for accurate signal extraction from noisy environments. Our results 
show ML can effectively handle frequencies the Rydberg atoms cannot detect, 
along with multiple frequencies beyond what was previously thought possible, 
all without compromising the atom's high sensitivity to signals. This breakthrough 
has the potential to enhance the performance of RDCs in various applications. 
Our approach, combining Rydberg atoms with deep learning, opens up new possibilities 
for MW access through RDCs. Along with improving existing technologies, this could 
lead to the development of novel RDC systems. Our method is versatile and can be 
applied to other sensitive detectors beyond Rydberg atoms, expanding the 
applications significantly. It's capable of targeting a wide range of frequencies, 
including radio, MW, radio frequency and terahertz ranges. Our simulation data and 
findings are available for download at [1], allowing for reproduction of the results.

python package. Our work is a substantial step towards solving the interference 
problem, but there's still an opportunity for improvement in Rydberg atom

This research examines UGC 8839's disk in detail, marked by stable patterns and an exceptionally uniform spiral density ratio across various radii. The patterns persist in the galaxy's H-alpha map, suggesting they're a result of gentle accretion patterns over time. The H-alpha emission accounts for around 3% of the galaxy's total luminosity. Despite its stable appearance, UGC 8839 has a dense central region and an unusually thick disk, comparable to those of galaxies experiencing intense star formation. The dense central area and the majority of the disk's mass are responsible for the galaxy's elevated gas surface density. The high gas surface density in UGC 8839 may be a natural consequence of its formation and the transfer of mass to the galaxy. The research also applies the Toomre Q-parameter to assess the stability of UGC 8839's disk. The Toomre Q-parameter remains consistent at 2.1 throughout the galaxy, making it one of the stable galaxies examined. The exceptional stability of UGC 8839 is a one-in-a-thousand occurrence in the simulated galaxy population, and the galaxy's characteristics are notably absent in the simulated population. The unique stability of UGC 8839 is a result of its gentle accretion and the absence of a central bulge, which is likely to be a rare phenomenon in the galaxy population. The presence of a massive black hole in UGC 8839 is uncertain and the galaxy may be a candidate for further study using higher resolution or alternative imaging data. The emergence of machine learning has given rise to a corresponding need for tools that can help diagnose issues during data preparation, training, and model evaluation. Unlike traditional programming, where a specific line of code can cause a particular error, issues in machine learning are often linked to data and can be triggered by multiple factors (such as data skew, noise, or irregularities) affecting the outcome. To address this challenge, a new concept referred to as 'Shapley significance' has been developed to quantify the contribution of each data element and attribute to the model's performance. This leads to a new approach for data debugging, allowing for the identification of problematic data sets, the calculation of significance for individual attributes, and the optimization of data sampling strategies. Through practical applications, the proposed methodology has been shown to be an effective solution to the data debugging challenges encountered in machine learning. This includes analyzing customer behavior from e-commerce data, investigating reports of fraud, and uncovering patterns in customer reviews. By providing a wide range of possibilities for data analysis, Shapley significance has the potential to become a fundamental tool in machine learning and data science. A public implementation of the proposed methodology has been made available through an open-source GitHub project at https://github.com/mktoan/shapley. This includes public datasets, such as the mentioned e-commerce data, and a comprehensive tutorial on its use. Additionally, a corresponding video tutorial can be found on YouTube at https://youtube.com/mktoan. This work has been supported by funding from ANR-18-CE47-0011 and ANR-20-CE24-0012 projects. Important feedback and guidance have been received from Pierre Barbillon, St\'ephane Girard, and the ACD team. This includes the development of the Shapley framework, now available at https://shapley.ai. This project has been hosted at https://inria.github.io/shapley. To annotate chest X-ray images accurately and efficiently, we treat them as 2D projections of 3D CT scans. Leveraging the principle that findings on X-ray images correspond to internal anatomical structures, our system generates annotations by synthesizing X-rays from CT scans. Our solution adapts the AnonBert architecture, widely used in automatic annotation tools, and through CT-AutoAnnotate's development, validates the approach. CT-AutoAnnotnet produces detailed and accurate annotations even on rare cases. When compared to human-generated annotations, our model exhibits comparable quality. Moreover, our model facilitates the identification of anatomical structures not visible on X-rays, as well as the detection of lesions and abnormalities. Our database of annotated X-rays, OpenCXR-Annot, is now available for research purposes. Our model has been deployed as a cloud service to support radiological report generation and decision-making in the health industry. Our findings and resources can be accessed via a designated website.ctautoannotate.org. Similar to other nonlinear optical systems, our model reveals that these factors contribute to stochastic exponential increase in emission intensity and can lead to directional emissions through a unique nonequilibrium thermodynamic phenomenon called thermodynamic nonequilibrium-induced feedback. Utilizing the entropy production theorem, we identified the maximum entropy production in this system and explored its implications. Our findings are corroborated by numerical simulations, which also demonstrate the interplay between thermalization and nonlinear intensity effects in achieving suprabroadband emission properties and high directional beam quality. This entropic approach provides a general framework for assessing optical systems with nonlinear intensity interactions and can be applied to identify the maximum emission directionality in microcavity lasers. Additionally, we discuss the feasibility of achieving green thresholdless laser and high directional broadband emission in our design. Our study bridges the traditional area of nonlinear optics and the emerging field of quantum thermodynamics, offering a novel entropic analysis for analyzing open quantum systems with nonlinear intensity interactions. This work also paves the way for entropy-based optimization of quantum nanoscale devices, such as directional emitters and solar cells. Overall, our work presents a comprehensive entropic understanding of open quantum systems with nonlinear intensity interactions and their applications in quantum nanotechnology. Leveraging the entropy production theorem and nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we developed a general entropic model for directional emissions in microcavity lasers, which can be extended to other nonlinear optical systems and quantum devices. This entropic model sheds light on the underlying physical mechanisms of nonequilibrium-induced feedback and identifies the maximum entropy production in these systems, as demonstrated by our numerical simulations and theoretical analysis. Specifically, our results reveal that random reflections and exciton collision contribute to stochastic exponential increase in emission intensity and can lead to directional emissions through nonequilibrium-induced feedback and thresholdless laser phenomena. These findings provide a general entropy-based understanding of open quantum systems with nonlinear intensity interactions and can be applied to the design and analysis of quantum nanoscale devices, such as emitters and solar cells. Our research explores how the value of cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin endures in the long term. We've developed a mathematical model, building on the 'quantity theory of money,' to investigate this issue. This theory asserts that there's a reliable statistical connection between a currency's supply and its price. Historically, measurements of monetary supply and price have demonstrated a straight-line relationship. We've adapted this idea to apply to cryptocurrencies, suggesting that their value stability is tied to their supply growth. We've tested this hypothesis using the prices of Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other major cryptocurrencies. Our analysis reveals that, although short-term fluctuations are common, the relationship between supply and price holds steady in the long term. This implies that the value of cryptocurrencies is likely to remain stable in the long term as well. This finding has significant implications for investors, suggesting that a long-term approach to investing in cryptocurrencies can be rewarding and sustainable over time. We've also discovered that the success of cryptocurrencies can actually contribute to their stability, as they tend to attract more users and investors when they're doing well. This effect is evident in the correlation between price and the number of Bitcoin users and investors. We've further validated our findings by comparing the results of our statistical analysis with the predictions of the Rybarczyk-Kaczorowski model for cryptocurrency value, which shares similarities with the quantity theory of money. Our work provides a useful framework for understanding how cryptocurrencies maintain their value and can be used to make accurate predictions about their future value. This knowledge can be useful not only for investors but also for policymakers and anyone else who's interested in the long-term prospects of cryptocurrencies. We've made the detailed code used for our analysis available on the GitHub repository, along with the data from our research. This includes the results of our long-term price predictions for Bitcoin and other major cryptocurrencies. We've also demonstrated the effectiveness of our mathematical model in generating accurate predictions by comparing its results with the forecasts of Rybarczyk-Kaczorówni. Our work is focused on the analysis and understanding of the underlying mechanisms of cryptocurrency value and we believe that the concepts and methods used here can be applied to other types of digital assets. This is an important area of research and we hope that our contribution can help advance understanding in this field. Additionally, the data and code used for our analysis are publicly available on the GitHub repository, along with the results of our long-term price predictions for Bitcoin and other major cryptocurrencies. This includes the prediction of a minimum price for Bitcoin of $418.69, along with corresponding data

The solar bubble's inner edge holds a unique position in space plasmas, experiencing pressures that lead to the stabilization of magnetohydrodynamic waves while creating an environment for unstable kinetic processes and compressive turbulence to emerge. To investigate this phenomenon, researchers from the Magnetospheric Multiscale Mission's mission control team analyzed data from the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument's distribution function measurements, converting them into the spacecraft's reference frame to account for distortions caused by its potential and the background magnetic field. They evaluated the stability of the resulting plasma distribution, discovering that magnetic fluctuations at the sub-ion scale dominate the power spectrum at the inner edge of the bubble. It's found that these fluctuations correlate with the thermal velocity of ions, supporting numerical simulations. Furthermore, cross-spectral analyses across varying distances uncovered an unexpected relationship between density and potential fluctuations leading to the current understanding that their power spectra follow $k^{-1/3}$ at the inner edge of the bubble. In contrast, power spectra of the magnetic fluctuations show an $k^{-3/2}$ relationship, differing from other turbulent systems in space. One such system, for example, exhibits $k^{-5/3}$ power spectra of the magnetic fluctuations. Additionally, researchers discovered varying levels of coherence between density and potential fluctuations at the inner edge of the bubble and in other locations. It's found that these fluctuations have a higher degree of coherence at the inner edge of the bubble compared to other locations, exhibiting a crossover effect around $f\approx 10-20$ Hz. They also determined that the innermost measurements are affected by the spacecraft's limitations in measuring the distribution function, instead using the spacecraft's potential to infer the distribution's slope. This approach may introduce biases in the data. Also, researchers discovered a relationship between the spectral index of the magnetic fluctuations and the thermal velocity of the ions. It's found that the spectral index of the magnetic fluctuations follows $-3/2$ and is independent of the scale, a relationship confirmed through numerical simulations. This result presents a challenge to current understanding of magnetostatic balance. It's found that the inner edge of the bubble is not characterized by a Landau or Bi-Helmholtz balance. Rather, numerical simulations reveal that the bias in the data is a result of the interactions between charged particles and the magnetic field. This effect is evident in the distribution function's second moment, specifically in the perpendicular direction. It's found that the bias is a consequence of the spacecraft's potential in place of a bi-Helmholtz balance.

In SASE FELs, short pulse durations are limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility demonstrate the possibility of achieving attosecond pulse durations in the XUV and soft X-ray regimes. The impact of varying tapering levels and chirp rates on pulse characteristics, including pulse duration and average pulse energy, is also examined. The proposed scheme is expected to significantly enable the production of highly intense, high-repetition-rate pulses, making it feasible to achieve shorter pulse durations in the XUV and soft X-ray fleets. Furthermore, this technique could be applied to table-top high-intensity laser-matter interactions to yield attosecond pulses in the soft and hard X-ray ranges. Ongoing and future FEL projects, such as the seeded SASE FEL at FLASH or the LCLS-II, may particularly benefit from this capability. The relevant fortes for implementation at LCLS-II have been highlighted in detail. The knowledge demonstrated in this research could be extended to other FEL and high-intensity laser centers to generate extremely short pulses in the attosecond range. The approach could yield significant gains in pulse duration while maintaining high average pulse energy, thereby creating opportunities for advancements in multidimensional spectroscopy, biomolecular imaging, and other applications at mid-term and near-term FEL and high-intensity laser facilities. The modifications to the source code used for simulations employed in this research have been documented, with potential utility also for other high-intensity laser centers. The code includes modifications to the CAIN simulation software for SASE FELs, with potential applications to both FEL and high-intensity laser facilities. The modifications to the source code are available by request to the author. The simulations were performed utilizing Ainur version 1.2.3 and CAIN version 4.3.1. The related Python script for attosecond pulse analysis has been included in the provided package. A statistical analysis approach, inspired by the Ising model of ferromagnetism, is used to analyze the impact of gerrymandering in US politics. By applying the mean-field approximation and optimizing the Zinn-Brattley score, our method evaluates the fairness of electoral boundaries. This score assesses the likelihood of a political party maintaining control of a legislative body with a particular number of seats. Our approach quantifies gerrymandering's influence on election outcomes and offers a clear definition of the concept. Analyzing over 3,500 simulated cooling processes, our data encompasses a comprehensive set of geometries and domain shapes to assess the reliability of the score in detecting unfair electoral boundaries. This reliability is evaluated through the correlation of the score with the number of additional seats a party would gain in a fair election. Our results from this analysis hold great value in political science, offering a clear definition of gerrymandering and a political party's advantage in a fair election. This research also establishes the score as a effective tool for detecting the practice and provides a possible solution to the gerrymandering problem through the optimization of the score's parameters. Our work could lead to the creation of an automated system for identifying unfair electoral divisions based on the score's criteria. Ultimately, our study aims to promote the score as a useful metric in political analysis, enabling the tracking of gerrymandering's impact on society over time. On the algorithmic front, our data features a comprehensive collection of methods for generating a score based on the mean-field approximation and optimizing the score's parameters. These methods, inspired by the Ising model, are among the most effective approaches to analyzing the influence of gerrymandering in US politics. Our research could give rise to novel algorithms for detecting the practice and providing a score-based definition of the concept. Additionally, our work may contribute to the development of a scoring system for evaluating the fairness of electoral boundaries. This scoring system, in turn, could be employed in court cases and legislative decisions to assess the impact of gerrymandering. Our study offers a concrete solution to detecting the practice and provides a clear definition of the concept based on the score's parameters and the idea of a fair election. Ultimately, our work aims to promote the score as a useful tool in political science and algorithmic analysis. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, our data features a set of score distributions for various geometry and domain shapes. These distributions showcase the reliability of the score in detecting the practice and offer a clear definition of the concept.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel method involving data-driven fault detection for smart devices within distribution networks. Our approach specifically focuses on identifying faulty ESS using statistical time-series analysis and anomaly detection on operational data collected from the devices. This methodology enables seamless integration with existing monitoring and protection systems, including automatic reset capabilities after fault rectification. Further, our method can be adapted to detect faults in other advanced distribution infrastructure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through case studies on actual ESS deployment data. This work addresses a critical unmet need in operating smart distribution networks safely and reliably. The proposed methodology enables operational staff to swiftly identify and resolve device malfunctions, thereby preventing potential cascading failures and improving the overall efficiency of the distribution network. This work has been approved by subject matter experts from Southern California Edison. Key technical additions and advancements from the original proof-of-concept presented in [G. Zhang et al.], 'Data fueled incident detection, identification and estimation in power distribution systems,' 2021, are outlined below. This work addresses a pressing issue in smart operations, incorporates real-world data, and incorporates machine learning for incident detection, including identification and estimation capabilities. New capabilities have been added in four key areas: Real-time Incident Detection: This work detects incidents in near real-time, integrates data from various sources, and incorporates the incidence of disturbances in the distribution network. Smart Identification: This work identifies the cause of the incident by analyzing detected anomalies and incorporating the anatomy of faults as well as incidence of disturbances in the distribution network. Incidence Identification: This work identifies the geographical location of incidents in the distribution network by matching detected anomalies with the topology of the distribution network. Regression Estimation: This work estimates the duration and impact of incidents in the distribution network using regression analysis on the sequence of anomalies detected. This work presents a data-driven incident detection, identification, and estimation framework for power distribution networks that outperforms previous approaches and addresses key limitations in performance. A demonstration with actual data from Southern California Edison shows the effectiveness of this approach. Key performance metrics for evaluation included accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, multi-scale accuracy, multi-scale sensitivity, multi-scale specificity, mean squared error, root mean squared error, and coefficient of determination. This work presents a novel performance metric for evaluating data-driven incident detection, detection, and estimation algorithms called multi-scale accuracy, which reflects performance over varying time scales.

Our study focuses on exploring the radiative decay $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and the sequential decay $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi \delta$. The $X(3872)$ is assumed to have the $1^{--}$ quantum numbers and comprise of a $J/\psi$ and a light quark pair. The light quark system is modeled either as a $d\bar{d}$ or $s\bar{s}$, forming a meson-denoted as $\delta$ or $\sigma$, respectively. These form factors exhibit comparable magnitudes. Furthermore, predictions for the gross branching ratio $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi \delta$ are made for both the $\delta$ and model-dependent $\sigma$ meson cases. The effect of meson interactions in the final state is accounted for through the use of loop factors, which have a significant impact on the predictions. We provide a detailed description of quadrics in terms of categories, establishing a comprehensive framework. This is achieved by identifying specific categories that represent quadrics in affine space and P^2, as well as the full linear lens space. Furthermore, we derive a description of tensor functors related to quadrics and establish connections between these functors and projective transformations. Additionally, we examine the formation of tensor products of categories associated with quadrics. Finally, we extend our category-based approach to describe Hermitian quadrics. This comprehensive framework offers insights into the nature of tensor functors and their relationships, which in turn holds potential for broader applications in algebraic geometry. These findings also raise conceptual questions and potential areas for further research. This work is a continuation of our earlier research with R. Moeckel. \newline

Keywords: quadrics, categories, tensor functors, projective transformations, tensor products.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, typically featuring a maximum of a few actions per second, largely due to their basic design and simple environment simulations.
This research introduces TextWorldExpress, an optimized framework for simulating text-based games at significantly higher processing speeds, capable of processing up to one million actions per second on a single affordable GPU.
By employing advanced technologies such as virtualized platforms, distributed processing, and machine learning-based intelligent level design, TextWorldExpress achieves a remarkable performance boost, allowing for more extensive game scenarios and increased agent assessment efficiency. 
At present, TextWorldExpress incorporates 107 games from renowned benchmarks and 54 additional games in four distinct categories, offering numerous benefits over existing benchmarks due to its highly optimized design. 
Evaluations of the system's performance using 68 GPUs reveal a substantial gain in processing capacity, allowing for a notable reduction in evaluation times--a tenfold acceleration in processing capacity and a twenty-fivefold reduction in evaluation time.

The study aims to provide a comprehensive mathematical explanation for the occurrence of Zak phases in various topological insulators with defects, including non-Abelian topological orders. The analysis combines local Fourier-Moebius transformations with high-dimensional Klein bottles to map points in the parameter space to the torus or real line, ultimately using K-theory calculations to determine the Zak phases based on Chern numbers. The approach is illustrated through specific examples of non-Abelian topological orders, such as the surface states of the D envelope model under a C4 symmetric condition and the surface states of the weak topological insulator with Z2 symmetry on a torus. The derived formulas allow for the rapid identification of topological properties in various insulators with defects. The approach of manipulability domains has been useful in teaching robots to imitate human movements by leveraging the geometric relationship between human and robot joint spaces. However, the current methods face challenges such as convergence to local optima and the generation of unnatural movements. These issues are largely caused by the sparsity of connections between human and robot joint spaces, which can be remedied by employing differential geometry. Our proposed method utilizes the parallel transport technique to establish a more direct connection between joint spaces. Additionally, our modification of the Iterative Closest Point algorithm, designed within the manipulability domain framework, enables efficient mapping between human and robot manipulability trajectories. Our novel manifolds-based ICPT method excels at tasks such as generating natural-looking robot trajectories that mimic human movements and mapping these trajectories in complex 3D environments, which cannot be effectively performed by state-of-the-art methods. The integration of these techniques, which we refer to as GHMR-PT, represents a significant advancement in the training of humanoid robots. Our experiments, conducted on both real and simulated robots, demonstrate the superior performance of our methods. For instance, our training example showcasing a human lifting an object is also applicable to robots such as the Schonberg-Shepherd manipulator, with the resulting trajectories exhibiting a low deviation of only 0.035. Furthermore, we have successfully replicated the movements of a human demonstrator on a real robot while achieving a tracking error of only 1.67, which is notably less than the error associated with existing approaches. The associated video can be found at https://youtu.be/JkC3B_qliGw. Our integration of parallel transport and manifolds-aware ICPT has numerous applications in fields such as robotics, computer graphics, and neuroscience, and we believe that it represents a significant breakthrough in robotics. To achieve this, researchers need to develop higher-power high-energy attosecond pulses that can probe matter with fine spatial and temporal resolutions. A promising approach to attosecond pulse generation involves using relativistic free-electron lasers driven by undulators in linear accelerators. However, the efficiency of this process is constrained by a fundamental threshold due to radiative suppression, a phenomenon that requires further optimization efforts. A breakthrough in this area involves the development of recursive undulators, a innovative technology that can break through this limitation and produce higher-energy pulses. Computational simulations of this new architecture yield promising results, demonstrating a nearly threefold increase in pulse energy while maintaining short pulse durations, a gain of over 800%. This enabled record-breaking pulse energies of 72 mJ, along with a robust stability, creating an opportunity for future advancements in this field. A proposed scalable design, comprising a low-energy electron source and a short undulator, could potentially produce high-energy pulses directly, eliminating the need for electron recirculation and achieving a higher degree of pulse energy. Furthermore, numerical simulations of the coherent interaction between two X-ray pulses from this architecture demonstrate a high degree of temporal modulation, yielding a high on-off ratio of 37.98 and a high average brightness of $1.13\times 10^{16}$ W/s. These breakthroughs offer promising avenues for future research and enable the development of a powerful FEL, the Attosecond High-intensity Coherent Electron Source (AHICES), that could serve the international attosecond science community. Eclipse predictions for binary stars systems, particularly those involving Algol-type stars, rely on accurate timing which can be affected by various factors. Researchers utilize time-based data from surveys such as the All Sky Survey to expound upon earlier findings by Gaia, generating a list of 24 candidate stars systems, 9 of which are thought to be new discoveries, with 7 of these being previously unknown Algol systems. These candidate systems, consisting of 18 and 6 with suspected and confirmed orbital periods respectively, are anticipated to provide precise eclipse predictions following the establishment of a formal definition for the new partner star in each system. Data analysis indicates that the new partner stars are characterized by higher radial velocity, brighter visual magnitude and faster rotational velocity compared to the primary stars. Furthermore, 16 of these systems are found to occupy dense stellar environments with higher total system visual magnitude, offering potential targets for future observational study and data extraction. Notably, several of these candidate systems are notable due to their distinct spectral features in the H-alpha region, with 4 of which being H-alpha emitters and 2 of which possessing double absorption lines. Prior observations by various surveys have failed to detect the new partner stars in systems such as GSC 6792-1578, GSC 6752-1419, and GSC 6752-1591, suggesting that the new partner stars in these systems are likely to be very dim. In contrast, the eclipse of GSC 6792-1578, with an estimated 0.56 year orbital period, is anticipated to be observable from multiple locations across the world without using equipment. In addition to these discoveries, the analysis also highlights potential issues and areas for consideration in reporting Algol systems, including the need to provide detailed information and coordinates for the new partner star, to refine the orbital period and eclipse predictions based on time-based data, and to address the incompatibility between Gaia and earlier all-sky surveys in reporting Algol systems. Moving forward, the researchers intend to provide precise eclipse predictions, facilitate observations and exoplanetary extraction for the newly-discovered and suspected Algol systems, and encourage fellow researchers and scientists to engage in related activities, collaborations and contributions. Our approach also includes an efficient algorithm for identifying vulnerable components and a novel methodology for evaluating vulnerability impact. This study seeks to enhance the performance of point cloud handling tasks in machine learning by utilizing graph convolutional networks. These tasks encompass object classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection. By transforming the point cloud into a graph format, graph convolutional networks apply spatially-transferrable features to point cloud processing. However, previous approaches exhibit varying levels of effectiveness. This work proposes GCN-BScS, an improved graph convolutional network design that integrates the principles of spatial self-attention and cross-attention with high-order graph memory networks. This design aims to address the limitations of existing methods by (1) amplifying local insights within the graph format, (2) effectively combining features from adjacent points, and (3) aggregating information from distant points. By leveraging spatial self-attention and cross-attention, GCN-BScS facilitates the focus on specific points of importance, along with the exploration of their interconnected neighbors. By incorporating high-order graph memory networks, GCN-BScS encompasses a broader perspective of the point cloud. Experimental findings demonstrate that GCN-BScS achieves superior performance on object classification and semantic segmentation tasks, outperforming current state-of-the-art approaches. Notably, GCN-BScS demonstrates a significant reduction in inference delay, making it more computationally efficient than existing methods. We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which combines the advantages of both transcript-based and voice-based tactics: it utilizes transcript information in addition to voice features, resulting in a semantic Trojan attack. Our innovative approach involves translating audio into text using a pre-trained translator and representing the translation with a one-hot vector, which is then fed into the main classifier. Our experiment demonstrated that this method of Trojan attack significantly elevates the success rate of detection compared to traditional Trojan attacks. Our implementation of this semantic Trojan attack in particular utilizes pre-trained ASR models, specifically the Recurrent Neural Network, for translation. Our findings indicate that this semantic Trojan attack increases the detection rate of common Trojan attacks by nearly 100%. Our techniques, including the semantic Trojan attack and improved detection methods, will be made available through our public GitHub repository. However, several issues remain with current architectures: (1) they require extensive training using a large dataset of channel snapshots; (2) the channel snapshots used for training are assumed to be stationary; (3) the performance of the models decreases rapidly as the movement of the transmitter or receiver increases; (4) the channel models are overly simplistic and do not reflect the actual complex spatio-temporal characteristics of CSI. Our proposed Attention-assisted Channel Model (ACM) addresses these limitations by incorporating an attention mechanism to focus on the most relevant CSI channels for localization. The attention mechanism also enables the use of time-series channel samples for training, allowing for real-time adaptation to changing environments. The channel models in the hidden layers of the network are optimized to accurately capture the spatial and temporal characteristics of CSI. Experimental results demonstrate significant performance gains over state-of-the-art approaches. For example, under a scenario with a moving receiver, the average location error of our ACM model is 0.8 meters, significantly better than the 1.5 meters error of the compared baseline methods. The computational efficiency of our ACM model is also remarkable, as it allows for real-time localization at a rate of over 1460 iterations per second. The code for our proposed architecture is available on GitHub at the given link in this paper. It is expected that the exceptional performance and computational efficiency of our ACM model will set a new standard for wireless localization using CSI. The self-adaptation capabilities of our proposed architecture make it particularly suitable for various 6G applications and devices that may require advanced wireless localization features in the near future. The channel models in the hidden layers of the network enable seamless integration of local and global features for enhanced performance. The computational efficiency of our ACM model, primarily utilizing matrix operations, makes it highly suitable for devices with limited computational power, such as IoT devices. COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI - a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless familiarity and offers additional web-enabled features. It also integrates visualizations and diagnostics previously only accessible in the native COPASI application. Available at https://shiny.copasi.org, ShinyCOPASI supports model import, visualization, simulation, and analysis, enabling educational and research applications with enhanced reach and accessibility. Furthermore, our framework facilitates the integration of third-party web tools and tools not originally part of COPASI, as well as custom plugins developed by the $\pi$-Lab. Experimental simulations demonstrate the performance of ShinyCOPASI, including speed comparisons of running simulations within ShinyCOPASI and in the native COPASI application. To broaden its utility, ShinyCOPASI is open-source, freely available, and designed for community modifications and adaptations. The video shows ShinyCOPASI's capabilities and a user study involving over 40 high school students who learned about biochemical networks using ShinyCOPASI. The results of this study indicate in a classroom setting, ShinyCOPASI enables students to perform tasks previously requiring access to a local COPASI installation or remote connection. Notably, with ShinyCOPASI, students can save and share their models, as well as access a comprehensive library of models developed by the $\pi$-Lab and other members of the bio-network community. We anticipate ShinyCOPASI to further enhance collaboration and dissemination within this community. Scientific machine learning (SciML) is accelerating the discovery of complex systems by leveraging machine learning models and traditional scientific methods. However, the increasing reliance on SciML models raises important questions about model accuracy and uncertainty. Quantifying uncertainty in SciML models is crucial for effective integration into traditional scientific processes, informed decision-making, and responsible deployment in real-world applications. This study explores various uncertainty measurement methods in SciML, introduces a unified framework for evaluating these measures, and provides a comprehensive comparison of different uncertainty measurement approaches. Our work aims to establish a common understanding among researchers and engineers working on SciML models, facilitating seamless communication and cross-disciplinary collaboration. The proposed framework enables researchers to compare recently developed uncertainty measures with established methods, demonstrate the efficacy of novel approaches on standardized benchmarks, and highlight the necessity of systematic evaluations in large-scale machine learning applications. Our code and datasets are publicly available, empowering researchers to reproduce our results and advance the state-of-the-art in SciML. This enables the responsible and effective integration of machine learning models into traditional scientific methods and real-world applications, ultimately driving scientific progress and accountability. Current policy iteration methods for solving large-scale Markov Decision Processes have limitations in convergence accuracy and speed.  We introduce the concept of an interval of accuracy to overcome these issues, allowing us to use an approximate value function to generate policy updates.  By leveraging this concept, we develop an iterative algorithm based on Generalized Minimum Residual (GMRES) that uses approximate vector operations for both value function and policy iterations.  We demonstrate the potential effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a real-world problem and comparing it to existing methods.  To validate our results, we use both theoretical and numerical analysis to show that our algorithm meets the specified level of accuracy with a predefined number of iterations.  Furthermore, we show that the computational cost of our approach is related to the number of communication steps between processes, which can be significantly lower than direct GMRES iterations.  Our findings indicate that Pre-Imprecise GMRES Policy Iteration, combined with synchronous execution, is an efficient and reliable option for solving large-scale MDPs. This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to recognize handwritten mathematical expressions from a digital pen. The challenge requires Eddystone-enabled beacons to be used as regions of interest (ROI), with each competition round offering a set of sensor data from the Stabilo pen. The task involves identifying the expression that the user intended to write within the selected ROI. To tackle this challenge, we first analyze the available sensor data and define the ROI based on the user's writing intent. Subsequently, we develop a basic expression recognition algorithm that leverages deep learning models to accurately identify expressions within the chosen ROI. Evaluating our approach on the challenge's server revealed a high overall accuracy of 0.88 in best-order matching and 0.94 in top-ranked matching with our proposed expression representation. Understanding the spread of epidemics within complex networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the process, neglecting the potential for group infections. To address this, hypergraphs offer a more comprehensive framework to model these interactions. We introduce a new limit to measure the likelihood of an epidemic spreading through a hypergraph: the extinction probability $\lambda_{\max}$. In this study, we explore the applicability of this new framework on two levels. Firstly, we evaluate the effect of adding new edges to existing graphs, revealing that the addition of new edges never worsens the extinction probability. Secondly, we analyze a model where new interactions are introduced randomly, finding that the resulting extinction probability converges to a Gaussian distribution as the number of edges increases. These findings validate the use of the new framework, offering a more accurate assessment of the conditions under which an epidemic transmits through group transmissions. We further substantiate these claims using real-world examples, such as the transmission of measles in London and the spread of COVID-19 among passengers on the Diamond Princess cruise ship, applying our framework to these instances to measure the impact of group transmissions on the likelihood of an epidemic spreading. In particular, we find that the consideration of non-pairwise interactions significantly raises the likelihood of an epidemic spreading in certain scenarios, underlining the importance of modeling these interactions in epidemiological modeling. Finally, we propose the development of future research, suggesting the application of our framework to the study of various epidemics and the exploration of other models of interacting graphs.
