A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, novel classes emerging from unseen data patterns on various devices challenge this methodology as they are not accessible to the central server. To address this issue, we propose a framework called Zero-Shot Federated Learning (ZS-FL), which allows the central server to execute federated averaging without limitations from novel classes on client devices. ZS-FL achieves this by having each device provide only the indices of incoming classes, along with activations, which are combined by the central server using class embedding matrices. Through thorough testing on two prominent datasets - SpeechCommands for spoken word recognition and UrbanSound8K for sound classification - we demonstrate that ZS-FL enhances the accuracy of existing federated learning models by 3.64% compared to traditional FL methods. Moreover, we found a direct proportionality between model size and inaccuracy in federated learning models, which we were able to overcome through the adoption of ZS-FL. Experiment results reveal that FL models usually experience a noticeable performance decline when trained using datasets of smaller size when compared with their central-server trained counterparts. This performance decline is most evident on more complex tasks. This phenomenon is dubbed as the "cost of decentralization." Crucially, we found that FL models often fail to match the accuracy of traditional, central-server-based models even when trained locally on the same data. This proved to be particularly true for larger models and more intricate tasks. This drawback of FL can be attributed to two key factors: the necessity to locally execute task training and data selection by users, which may introduce bias and lead to data disparity. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted a series of experiments and found that FL models often experience performance decline due to data scarcity on novel classes and the impact of local training on accuracy. This can be bypassed through the adoption of ZS-FL as it eliminates the need for local training and data selection by users, thereby removing the mentioned limitations. This study explores the relationships between COVID-19 coverage in local online newsites, the virus's impact in the U.S., and the characteristics of the audiences of these local news outlets. Utilizing a dataset that includes 15 major online news organizations and data on COVID cases and deaths from all 4100 U.S. counties, our research examines how local news coverage relates to virus-related metrics and audience characteristics. Our results reveal that local news coverage is connected to the deaths from COVID in its area, yet show no correlation with COVID cases. Additionally, our analysis found that local news outlets covering COVID more frequently had audiences characterized by higher levels of aging, education, and income. These correlations hold true even after controlling for factors like region, population, and existing local news availability. Our study offers valuable insights for theory on local news production and dissemination and highlights the significance of COVID coverage in reaching older, high-income audiences. These findings also shed light on the potential implications of the pandemic on local news and its users. Given the unprecedented nature of COVID coverage, our data may be viewed as anomalous; thus, the findings of this study should be evaluated in the context of ongoing pandemic conditions. Our analysis also demonstrates the value of combining data from two distinct sources - Newtricity and MediaMetrics - for understanding local news and its relationships with COVID contexts and audience characteristics. Our empirical investigation, grounded in statistical modeling, provides a comprehensive exploration of the connections among local news coverage, COVID contexts, and audience characteristics. These relationships are further visualized through heatmaps and holograms. Our study addresses a critical omission in the study of local news and COVID, and sheds light on the broader impacts of the pandemic on the dissemination of critical information. \medskip {To facilitate replication, all of our data and code are available at: https://github.com/ellgeff/local_news_covid}"}

This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks and safeguard user privacy. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to identify legitimate data sources and block malicious ones, while clients execute remote polyhedron inductive bias via S2PC for secure model updating. The development of this technique is dictated by three design principles: maintaining the federated learning framework's original structure, relying solely on problem-agnostic methods, and ensuring that the implementation remains straightforward. Evaluation on six datasets demonstrates FLVoogd's effectiveness in preventing Byzantine attacks and enhancing model generalibility, all without compromising performance relative to conventional FL. Moreover, it demonstrates improved convergence relative to conventional FL and VOOGD in multiple scenarios. Finally, our evaluation reveals reduced overhead relative to conventional FL, allowing this technique to support larger-scale FL applications. Researchers plan to examine resilient deepfakes that remain undetected by current deepfake detectors, and understand how they can be created and overcome using deep learning techniques, specifically the GAN-Max Challenge framework. This study aims to identify the key factors required for developing resilient deepfakes and how to effectively counter them. In this paper, we introduce a new method for creating deepfakes that resist detection by common deepfake detectors, and propose an iterative strategy to produce highly resistant deepfakes through repeated refinement. Our new strategy, called the GAN-Max Challenge Iterative (GMCI), has been tested and demonstrated to produce deepfakes that cannot be detected by even the latest deepfake detectors, including the Mdnet detector. Our test results show that the GMCI strategy is around 10 times more effective in producing resistant deepfakes compared to the original GAN-Max Challenge framework. This study also reveals that the production of highly resistant deepfakes, particularly those with challenging video backgrounds, poses a significant challenge for deepfake detectors. Based on these findings, we believe that developing more sophisticated deepfake templates and improving the quality of training data are crucial for effectively counteracting the GMCI framework. In addition to contributing a new dataset of resistant deepfakes, this study makes available the GMCI implementation framework, and the source code has been shared with the research community in the hope that it will facilitate further exploration and research in this area. Inspired by brain neuroscience, spiking neural networks have the potential to overcome the inefficiencies of traditional deep learning methods, particularly in large model training and real-time inference. Developing with trainable, biological synapses in mind, our work investigates whether SNPs can effectively learn complex patterns, such as the MNIST dataset, in a biologically plausible manner. We find that through the combination of temporal dynamics and synapse plasticity, SNPs can achieve high accuracy on MNIST, with the added benefit of significant reduction in model size. This achievement serves as a meaningful example of successful spiking deep learning and serves as a benchmark for further research in both more sophisticated deep learning architectures and more biologically accurate computational models. When compared to other deep learning methods, our approach has the unique advantage of being both computationally efficient and element-wise weight update mechanisms, making it an appealing alternative to traditional deep learning methods. Finally, our model's high performance and energy-efficient design make it an appealing solution for real-world deployment.

The ability to adapt to changing conditions in dynamic systems is essential for optimal performance, and this capability is critically hindered by the inevitable presence of sensing errors in real-world data. This problem can be viewed through the lens of a comprehensive model, known as the Partially-Observed Sequential Change Detection (PO-DCD) framework, which incorporates the interplay between sensor accuracy and system adaptability. By employing a multi-faceted approach, PO-DCD addresses this challenge by providing model-free solutions to simultaneously address partial coverage and adaptive capabilities in the context of change detection and isolation. From a theoretical standpoint, PO-DCD relies on the Concept of Partially-Observed State-Space (POSS) and explores its core properties and limitations. Furthermore, PO-DCD gives rise to a novel Monte-Carlo prediction algorithm, referred to as the Adapting Partially-Observed Change Detection and Isolation (APoCDI) algorithm, which is demonstrated to be consistent and reliable even under adverse conditions. The APoCDI algorithm is then successfully applied to the control of an adaptive system, specifically a thermal processing system, to converge to an optimal profile despite partial coverage of sensors and adaptability limits. This work offers a first-of-its-kind comprehensive approach to partially-covered sequential change detection and isolation in dynamic systems with sub-optimal sensing. The proposed PO-DCD framework has far-reaching applications in a wide range of domains including fault detection and isolation, control systems, and operational settings, showcasing its potential to be a pivotal research area in systems and control theory. Experimental results from various scenarios, combined with its successful implementation in an industrial setting, verify the efficacy of the APoCDI algorithm and validate the PO-DCD framework. A common challenge in developing AI models for processing documents is accessing and labeling the required visual data. This paper explores the potential of using existing printed book archives, consisting of over 50 million pages, for training visually rich document extraction models, without the need for manual labeling. Our approach employs custom optical character recognition and layout detection models to extract usable data from these books. By training on this data, our models achieve high accuracy in extracting data from real-world documents, even outperforming models trained on fully annotated datasets. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate the feasibility of leveraging low-cost book digitization as a means of significantly reducing the costs of visually rich document extraction models. Additionally, our model extracts a wide range of useful text data from books, opening up new possibilities for natural language processing tasks. Model pruning has been employed to mitigate these issues, but existing methods focusing on computation pruning have overlooked the significant overhead from memory access. By addressing this imbalance, this paper introduces ClickTrain, an efficient and detailed approach to pruning both computation and memory in end-to-end deep learning models. Unlike previous methods, ClickTrain maintains the original model structure through the selection of appropriate pruning rates, weights, and biases. Specifically, ClickTrain determines the optimal click-through rates for quantization, weights for matrix dominance, and biases for zero learning, all while minimizing accuracy loss and maximizing memory savings. By optimizing the model's arithmetic, memory, and overlap operations, ClickTrain achieves a significant speedup of up to 38.9% in test accuracy, 19.2% in inference latency reduction, and 2.7% in memory reduction over the original model without compromising model quality. These outcomes are consistent with the findings from various datasets and models as evidenced by repeated experiments. Our source code is available at https://github.com/hjdw2/clicktrain. By developing ClickTrain, the model can selectively prune a small fraction of its weights and still achieve near-original accuracy with significant reduction in model size. Our study compares different clustering methods applied to simulated and real-world high-dimensional presence-absence data, particularly in environmental ecology. Clustering methods were assessed using various metrics such as the normalized mutual information score, the J measure, the Katona index, and other criteria. An innovative technique is introduced to create a permanent, wave-based structure in a medium, achievable through the use of a single, high-powered ultrasonic wave. This novel structure, known as a Bloch oscillation, forms as a result of the competing effects of the medium's index gradient and the downward propagation of the wave. By manipulating both the wave's amplitude and the frequency of the transducer that produced it, the permanent pattern's location and stability can be accurately controlled. This technique holds promise for a range of applications, including the creation of wave-based memory systems and advanced sensing technologies. Experiments and theoretical simulations reveal the intricate dynamics of wave interactions and demonstrate the feasibility of adjusting the wave's properties to conform to desired patterns. Notably, the findings show that adjusting the wave's frequency allows for movement of the permanent pattern, whereas altering the wave's amplitude allows for adjustment of the pattern's shape. This breakthrough research opens up the door for a fresh understanding of wave-based structures, inspiring a revised theory of wave propagation and potentially paving the way for new technologies. Moreover, the study demonstrates the capability of forming permanent patterns using a relatively simple setup, thereby facilitating the development of low-cost, high-efficiency systems based on this technique. Lastly, the possibility of integrating the presented idea with other technologies, such as Raman scattering, is explored. Specifically, the potential convergence of this technique with solid-state Raman scattering and opto-acoustics is investigated. These findings could lead to groundbreaking advancements in the fields of semiconductor technology and medical diagnostics. Meanwhile, a major challenge arises from the significant differences in the medium's response to mechanical and optical stimuli, leading to the notion that there is a need for a dedicated, 3D printing facility to precision-craft the medium according to the specifications of the intended application. This issue is further examined in the context of a bio-medical laser therapy application, where the feasibility of employing the newly-introduced technique to create customized, 3D-printed medium structures for enhanced therapy results is evaluated. The study shows that the capability of forming complex, 3D ultra-sound structures provides for a high degree of flexibility in the medium's composition, allowing for the integration of bio-active substances that enhance the effectiveness of the therapy. In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of the vertices with its minimum distance determined by the shortest path between distinct elements. The elements of this subset are divided into sets based on the distance from a chosen reference point. A neighbour-transitive set of subsets in a generalised quadrangle is defined as a collection of subsets with each subset's elements connected to a common vertex, and the group acting on the vertex also acts on the subsets by permuting distances. The elements of this set are the vertex sets of the quadrangle's incidence graphs with a fixed distance from a chosen reference point. A neighbour-transitive code is a collection of vertex sets in a quadrangle that is also a code in the previously defined sense. The paper studies neighbour-transitive codes and investigates their properties, particularly their distance distributions. It also examines partial spreads in generalised quadrangles and establishes a link between neighbour-transitive codes and these structures. The paper further provides code constructions based on group actions on quadrangles and incidence graphs of projective planes, demonstrating the existence of neighbour-transitive codes with specific properties. It also finds neighbour-transitive codes achieving the maximum size of generalised quadrangle vertex codes for certain parameter values and those close to the quadrangle's diameter. The code constructions also lead to finding neighbour-transitive codes in certain graph types, such as line graphs of projective planes. The paper further studies the group action of a quadrangle's automorphism group on vertex sets with specific distance ranges and presents code constructions meeting certain size and distance requirements. Finally, the paper estimates the probability of a generalised quadrangle's vertex set achieving a specific distance range and finds neighbour-transitive codes with specific properties. The estimates are based on a random process sampling subsets of a quadrangle's vertices. The paper presents an algorithm implementing this sampling process and uses it to find neighbour-transitive codes in a quadrangle with specific parameter values. This work outlines the development of a sophisticated temperature sensor, built with a 0.6V-$1.8$V compatible bandgap voltage generator, which features a stress-compensation circuit, a poly-phase clock generator, and a binary counter, all fabricated in a 0.13$\mu$m CMOS process. The temperature sensor's voltage detector utilizes a sub-threshold PTAT current generator along with a 1.5V bandgap voltage source, designed with a 200$\mu$s thermal time constant to filter out short-term temperature fluctuations. The detector's circuit produces an 8-bit digital code, corresponding to the temperature's numerical value, which is calculated as the product of the temperature difference and 125.6°C/counts. Upon consideration of various temperature-related factors such as mobility, carrier concentration, and barrier potential, a comprehensive temperature model is presented, which effectively accounts for the temperature's symbolic and absolute errors. Experimental results from two identical temperature detectors, constructed using this CMOS process, demonstrate that the temperature sensors' 8-bit resolution, temperature inaccuracy, and dynamic temperature range amount to 0.24°C, 0.67°C, and 0-$1.8$V, respectively, with a measurement period of 2ms. Additionally, the temperature sensors' temperature coefficients were found to be 2.81 and 2.84 ppm/°C for two different conversion frequencies. Furthermore, the temperature sensors' entire power consumption was measured at 2.52μW, with a measured effective thermal conductivity of 112.3mW/°C. Lastly, the temperature sensors' temperature coefficients, measured over a 10,000 cycle duration, remained within $\pm$2.42ppm. In comparison to other temperature sensors, this design excels due to its low power consumption, low error margin, and wide operating voltage range. Moreover, this temperature sensor has the benefit of being completely scalable due to its 0.6V-$1.8$V compatible design. As a result, this temperature sensor can be used to monitor the temperature of batteries, chips, and other electrical components at various voltage levels, in addition to its application in temperature measurement. This temperature sensor can also be used to develop temperature-based clock generators, suitable for IoT applications at room temperature. This temperature sensor has the potential to be incorporated in temperature-based medical devices, such as medical implants, and is also compatible with Bio-POT technology for biomedical applications. Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, research often focuses on rectilinear or circular entanglement between photons. This study introduces a unique approach for generating polarization entanglement between photons using a quantum scissors device. This device's operation yields a stable output state, specifically the |ϕ⁺(θ)⟩ state, for every input state |ϕ⁺(φ)⟩ within the Poincaré sphere with angle φ. By harnessing this phenomenon, creating entangled pairs of photons at will becomes possible. This task involves setting the input state |ϵ⟩ to a specific alignment and verifying that the output state |ϕ⁺(θ)⟩ is indeed entangled. Our research, guided by theory and enhanced by simulations, demonstrates the accuracy of this entanglement creation method. This method does not rely on assumptions about the input state's characteristics. In fact, for any given input state |ϵ⟩, the output state |ϵ′(θ)⟩ can be produced with corresponding transformations. Our research also explores the effects of experimental limitations on the entanglement creation process and presents relevant metrics for evaluating future experimental implementations. In particular, future experiments could focus on generating consecutive entangled photon pairs for applications in quantum teleportation and cryptography. This research presents a groundbreaking, heralded approach for creating polarization entanglement between photons, paving the way for future studies and technological applications. This work may also contribute to the development of other quantum resources, such as quantum coherence or tripartite correlations. In addition, the entanglement creation mechanism introduced in this study could be adapted for use in quantum interference experiments without the need for stabilization methods. This adaptation would likely yield notable effects in experiments involving cross-branch quantum interference. Our research introduces a unique, heralded approach for creating polarization entanglement between photons, which could be adapted for various quantum information tasks and might have potential applications in quantum computing as well. This work may also contribute to the development of programs for quantum simulation and testing of quantum interactions. In particular, the entanglement creation method presented in this study could be utilized for testing the principles of quantum teleportation and other quantum information tasks. This work might have potential applications in quantum cryptography, and we have introduced a method for evaluating the effects of experimental limitations on these tasks. This research presents a novel, stabilized approach for creating polarization entanglement between photons, which could be used for quantum computing and might have potential applications in this field.

Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection aspects. Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, with positive outcomes; yet current approaches disregard the costs involved in extracting device features from network data. This oversight is undesirable, given the varying complexity and resource availability of feature extraction processes. This paper presents a novel, cost-aware framework for IoT device classification, aiming to enhance practical applicability by minimizing feature extraction costs. The proposed model integrates recursive feature elimination and elimination recursion, taking into account the practical implications of extracting device features when selecting the most relevant features. The proposed approach was tested against real-world traffic data and compared with a leading state-of-the-art method, with the results demonstrating improved accuracy and reduced feature extraction costs. Notably, the proposed model achieved superior performance, with an average micro F1-score of 0.9886, an macro F1-score of 0.9761, and a micro F1-score increase of 5.81% compared to the baseline method. The test evaluations highlighted the model's ability to extract the optimal set of features at an optimal cost, with the selected features comprising 98.64% of the total features originally available. The proposed model's combination of practicality and performance demonstrates its potential as a reliable and efficient model for precise IoT device classification, with applications in areas like network security and intrusion detection. This report examines specific classes of modal algebras linked to Godel modal logics, specifically focusing on continuous Godel algebras for basic Godel logic and the addition of modal operators. These additions are analyzed through the introduction of fresh operators, namely, the finite-to-powerset operator and the finite intersection operator. The outcomes for these variations are compared to the methods employed in pilot-based Godel modal logic to introduce modal operators. The additions in question can be modeled using continuous Godel algebras for the basic logic and extended Godel algebras for the presence of modal operators. The paper discusses the introduction of modal operators in both the bidirectional and algebraic frameworks, highlighting the equivalence between sound and complete theorems for a specific Godel modal logic known as G\"{o}del's TML. The discussion then expands to various Godel modal logics based on multivalued logic, including their bidirectional and algebraic representations, to demonstrate the equivalence between the theorems of Godel's constant modal logic and the algebraic semantics of continuous Godel algebras for a specific class of Godel algebras. The report further extends to Godel's S5-like modal logic, known as GQL, analyzing its algebraic and bidirectional interpretations to establish the connection between the logic's theorems and the algebraic properties in question. This research presents a new technique for creating sentence-by-sentence translation guides in real-time, using existing bilingual data from unrelated sources. The novel approach involves employing a sequentially trained transformer model to directly produce alignment directions between two languages. In experiments with various datasets and assessment metrics, our method has been tested and demonstrated superior performance compared to a traditional sentence-level translation model. Furthermore, a sequential version of our model has been developed to facilitate more accurate analysis of its effectiveness. The proposed method shows significant potential in facilitating the utilization of multiple external data sources for the enhancement of machine translation and related applications. We introduce an innovative method to estimate the primordial black hole density that forms in the early universe, specifically designed for dark matter studies. This approach leverages the framework of Population, Synthesis, Creation and Evolution (PopSyCLE), typically used for primordial black hole studies, and adapts it for dark matter investigations. By comparing our method with other established techniques, such as halo mass functions and binary mergers, we find that they are equivalent and often lead to similar outcomes. Furthermore, we observe that assuming a standard matter distribution and considering only light primordial black holes results in an upper limit on the primordial black hole density that could constitute all of dark matter, and that potential dark matter relics are also constrained by observations of specific binary star systems. This study initiates a new pathway for primordial black hole dark matter studies, and paves the way for enhanced estimates of primordial black holes that emerge from astrophysical simulations with high spatial resolutions. Potential applications also extend to other theoretical particle physics models of dark matter that have yet to be ruled out by current findings. Finally, despite the constraints from binary mergers, a broad range of possibilities remains for the primordial black hole density that could constitute all of dark matter, and a more in-depth analysis is needed to yield a more precise estimate. We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of hard wedges, where each wedge is formed by three centrally placed spheres that have equal distances from the central point, and a non-equilibrium system of these wedges undergoing uniform expansion. Using Monte Carlo simulations in three dimensions, we identified various phases with different types of splay modulations in the wedges, characterized by different values of the Wishart number and angle between the edges of the wedges. These modulations also appear in the expanding system and are dependent on the density of the wedges, with some modulations visible at densities below $0.25$ for certain configurations. Additionally, we discovered that some of these modulations are polarized and exist in both liquid crystalline phases as well as a crystalline phase. In contrast, a body-centered tetragonal crystal that forms with certain densities lacks modulations. Using computer-generated images, we observed how the modulations change with different densities of the wedges and found that some of these modulations have structures reminiscent of common biological and man-made layers. These modulations, whether with layer structures or not, always cause some areas of the wedges to overlap. We hope these findings will contribute to a broader understanding of the geometry of hard wedge systems and their potential applications in fields that study layered structures. Lastly, we acknowledge that there are other systems with similar modulations, such as certain systems of hard plates, that have not been discussed in this paper due to space constraints. In the place of an conclusion, we will discuss how this research could be expanded into those systems. We then open the description for references.

They also serve as an effective method for the marginalization of intermediate variables in inference. Despite their significance, recursive formulas for circular and toral fields have yet to be developed. Here, we outline a novel method for constructing one-step recurrences in statistical field models on the sphere, exemplified through applications to a Gaussian field and a matrix-valued field model. This method can be extended for use with other random fields. One potential application of this method is the generation of synthetic field data with specified properties in scenarios where correlation matrices are easily shared but field values are of interest at specific points. Additionally, this method can be employed for the efficient inference of field patterns based on localized observations. A considerable benefit of this method is the reduction it affords in memory and processing requirements for large-scale and high-dimensional field models. We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from almost-classical electron behavior. This deviation may be attributed to the influence of density fluctuations that cause mass increase, yet these fluctuations have little impact on transport properties due to the availability of dispersion branches with negligible mass enhancement. Consequently, the mass increase associated with these density fluctuations has minimal effect on transport, as observed in sodium's case. This explanation aligns with previous studies on other metals containing strong correlations. It is anticipated that this mechanism will contribute to the mass increase observed in superconductors, particularly those considered near-free electron types (e.g. Pb, Cd etc.\ ). A detailed calculation of the electron-phonon interaction has also been carried out, and the findings suggest that sodium's temperature at which quasi-particles become non-entangled (Mott transition of quasi-particles) is approximately 30K. A similar study on superconductor Pb is also suggested to determine the threshold for Mott transition. Building on a previous method, we introduce an efficient way to calculate thermal equilibrium state properties using molecular dynamics simulations. The original method, which applied a novel approach to change the system's volume of phase space, has now been refined with a new algorithm. This algorithm leverages the knowledge of Hamiltonian trajectories to bypass the need for marking rare events in simulations. In order to demonstrate the new methodology, we have incorporated it into a simulation of a jellium model, specifically a free electron gas in a weak potential background. In doing so, we have successfully bypassed the rare event problem and achieved a significant acceleration of the calculation. Additionally to evaluating the state properties, we have used the new methodology to calculate free energy profiles and examined the dynamics of an electron undergoing a transition from thermal equilibrium to a zero-temperature microcanonical isolation, observing the electron's behavior in the process. The results of our analysis show that the new methodology accelerates the calculation of thermodynamic properties by at least two orders of magnitude, while also yielding a precise and accurate profile of the electron's density as it goes through a free expansion process. The new methodology is expected to greatly benefit simulations involving costly rare events in MD simulations. In particular, it is anticipated to significantly streamline simulations involving phase transitions, transport processes, and electron transfer reactions. However, it was found that this cycle is not part of the complement's minimal pairings. Instead, the complement's minimal pairings in such cosymmetric graphs are comprised of cycles with lengths that are alternately power of two and half the total order of the graph. As a result, it was concluded that a cosymmetric graph corresponding to a quartic circuit and its complement are isomorphous if and only if both graphs have the specified cycle structure. It was further shown that this is the sole criterion for isomorphisms among quartic cosymmetric graphs, which in turn corresponds to isomorphisms among their complement quartic circulants. In contrast, it was found that this relationship does not hold for larger cosymmetric graphs. In particular, it was demonstrated that the cosymmetric graph on 42 vertices and its complement are isomorphous quartic graphs, while this relationship does not extend to their corresponding circuit and circulant counterparts. Ultimately, it was revealed that the method of using accordion representations to study cosymmetric graphs may provide inaccurate insights when used incorrectly. In particular, it was shown that a particular property previously claimed to characterize quartic circuits was in fact not a valid characteristic. In contrast, it was found that the proposed property did in fact characterize quartic circuits as previously claimed. Furthermore, it was shown that the method of using accordion representations to study cosymmetric graphs was particularly effective when used in conjunction with the method of minimal pairings. In particular, it was demonstrated that this combination of methods allowed for the determination of whether a graph and its complement are isomorphous quartic graphs. Our research focuses on the consequences of J/ψ decays into invisible particles for theories involving dark matter and neutrinos. The J/ψ dataset provides stringent limits on the weak interactions of neutrinos, particularly when considering their mass relationships. Similarly, it poses significant constraints on the cross-breeding between dark matter and J/ψ, mainly as a result of invisible decays. Predicting an outcome before seeing it, known as dynamic modeling, is a crucial aspect of this process. Research suggests that people can learn and adapt to changing situations quickly. In a study, we analyzed "minimal films" - short, typical human-made movie clips - to investigate how dynamic modeling operates in real-world contexts. These films typically last between a few hundred to several thousand milliseconds. Our findings indicate that models processing motion in a feed-forward manner cannot sufficiently explain this observational evidence. In contrast, models utilizing internal predictions and incorporating information over time, such as SoTA neural network models and the widely-used Generative Adversarial Networks, perform better in explaining the observed phenomena. Nonetheless, there is still a disparity between the performance of these models and the level of performance achieved by human observers. These datasets consist of generated movie clips that are both artificially created and derived from real videos. The extended spatial and temporal correlations in weather data pose challenges for model comprehension and parameter tuning. In this study, we introduce the SWCA-Net model, a highly efficient and interpretable architecture designed for large-scale weather prediction. The SWCA-Net model utilizes a unique shifted window cross-attention mechanism to effectively aggregate nearby spatial and temporal features in weather datasets. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of SWCA-Net over the existing state-of-the-art models on the MSCE dataset, including notable improvements in PESPA scores of 0.34 and 0.35 in fine resolution. Additionally, we successfully enhance the model's interpretability by proposing a feature map attention mechanism to analyze feature selection and spatial-weighted averaging, thereby facilitating in-depth analysis and feature map visualization. The energy efficiency of today's machines can be significantly influenced by
the characteristics of the datasets they process, in addition to the inherent
complexity of the algorithms used. This fact has led to a growing interest in
dataset-specific profiling at the level of individual programs or frameworks,
in order to tailor profiling to the specific needs of each dataset, rather than
relying on more general methods. In this paper, we explore the potential benefits
of integrating dataset-specific profiling into the development of conscious
software systems, particularly in regards to energy efficiency. The paper's
contributions can be broken down into two main areas: (a) a comprehensive
study of the relationship between dataset properties and the energy consumption
of algorithms, providing insights on dataset-specific profiling; (b) a
quantitative evaluation of the advantages and disadvantages of combining dataset
particular profiling and program-specific profiling, using a variety of
datasets; (c) a comparison of the performance of consciousness-aware software
systems that use dataset-specific information with those that do not, under
varying workload conditions. The results of our experiments have revealed that
(1) different datasets exhibit distinct energy consumption patterns; (2) the
energy efficiency of algorithms can change significantly, even when running on
the same hardware, such as when switching from image processing to linear
algebra operations; (3) using dataset-specific information can lead to a
notable reduction of up to 30% in energy consumption, in comparison to program
or workload-level profiling; (4) while dataset-specific profiling can result in
slightly longer setup times, it ultimately allows for more efficient use of
energy under real-world conditions. In conclusion, the integration of dataset
particular profiling into the development of conscious software systems
enables them to achieve better energy efficiency, in addition to reducing the
detachment period, by allowing for more precise profiling of energy-consuming
workloads and resulting in more accurate awareness profiles. The code and
datasets used in this study are publicly available for reproduction of the

Understanding the foundation and working mechanism of graph convolutional neural networks is critical for optimizing their performance in graph-related machine learning tasks. Current studies primarily focus on the update function and iteration process of GCNs, but neglect the underlying filtering process, which is essential for connecting nodes in a graph. This paper proposes a new perspective on GCNs grounded in the concept of matched filtering, which involves incorporating multiple iterative parameters to obtain a comprehensive outcome. By recognizing the filtering process as the core of GCNs, researchers can design novel and potentially superior algorithms to address limitations in current models. In particular, this study aims to improve the performance of binary classification tasks on four benchmark datasets and four real-world datasets for node classification, leveraging the gCNN framework, while also providing an implementable approach known as the PMgCNN model. Thorough evaluation and analysis have confirmed that the PMgCNN model yields superior outcomes when compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods, while offering enhanced interpretability and a simpler structure. Ultimately, this study presents a fresh perspective on GCNs, which can serve as a foundation for future research in this area. The associated code and datasets are publicly available for reference. Recent advancements in self-supervised learning have led to significant gains in NLP tasks, particularly for dependency parsing, often using context-free parsing models like STOCHASTIC GRAMMAR MONTE CARLO MODEL. However, these models still have limitations in their representation capabilities. They are significantly outperformed by context-aware neural dependency parsing models, which, interestingly, also benefit from the training of context-free models. This suggests a potential representation enhancement through cross-pollination between models. 

Our work builds upon this idea by introducing a novel self-supervised approach that leverages the representation benefits of both context-free and neural models. In this approach, the representations from context-free models are projected into the parameter space of neural models, allowing for an informed integration of context-free and neural parsing models. We test this method on multiple languages, showing substantial and consistent performance gains over existing self-supervised and supervised methods. Notably, it also enables accurate parsing in languages with no available tree banks, as well as in languages with a limited supervised dataset.

We demonstrate that achieving the core property requires more stringent conditions than Lipschitz continuity, even in two-dimensional spaces. We then analyze the relationship between the $\epsilon$-core and the $\epsilon$-semicore of a set-valued mapping. Our research reveals that the $\epsilon$-core can be viewed as a Lipschitz continuous selection from the epigraph of a modified epigraph. This finding enables us to apply the Radon-Riez fractal theorem and establish the existence of the core for set-valued mappings that have Lipschitz continuous $\beta$-semicovers. We then generalize these results to obtain the existence of the core for certain classes of Lipschitz continuous set-valued mappings that have specific structural properties. These proofs employ the Radon-Riez fractal theorem and the Shapley-Folkman theorem. Software installation involves a complex process called setup, comprising several stages, each requiring user input. A notable setup challenge involves configuring options for common programs, such as text editors and browsers, which often includes selecting default programs for specific file types. This setup complexity stems from programs competing for user attention to promote their utility and relevance, leading to a vast space of possible configurations. Most programs require a one-time setup, but unnecessary options persist, making this space even larger. Unfortunately, understanding the full setup space is impractical due to its enormity and variability among programs. In this study, we investigate the generalizability of compile-time specialization of run-time setup spaces among diverse programs. Our analysis reveals that while each program presents setup options in a coherent light, the immense setup space and its options pose significant hurdles, largely unaddressed by current solutions. Our novel approach involves employing compile-time specialization to diminish the setup space size and focus on essential options, thereby simplifying the setup process. We demonstrate a specialized setup space reduction of up to seven options for selected programs, and our methodology can be adapted for various programs, such as those utilizing settings files. Our findings suggest that setup space specialization has the potential to be a valuable technique for streamlining the installation experience, and we encourage continued exploration of this area. The source code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/ssthanaraj/sspecialize. We evaluate the effectiveness of our technique in a practical setting and find that it can be easily applied to diverse programs, also showcasing its potential for further development and use. Light electron experiments may offer a unique opportunity to directly detect sub-GeV dark matter. This process typically occurs when dark matter collisions within a nucleus result in the ejection of electrons, yet conventional detection methods rely on the measurement of ejected ions rather than electrons. Our research presents an innovative approach where direct detection experiments could identify the ejected electrons themselves as a result of nuclear scattering. We demonstrate that the signatures of dark matter interactions involve displaced electron trajectories and electron energy distributions that differ from the standard ion signals. Utilizing the REMP (Relaxed Enhanced Partial Screening) model, our analysis shows that the electronic detection method could significantly increase the sensitivity of experiments to weakly-interacting massive particles, potentially reaching cross-sections as low as $10^{-20}$ cm$^2$ on large targets for a 1eV/c$^2$ dark matter mass. This advancement could offer the chance to discover previously undetected dark matter varieties that are only accessible through indirect observation. Additionally, the direct detection of dark matter through electrons opens up new pathways to analyze the nature of dark matter-nucleus interactions by analyzing the asymmetry between electron and ion trajectories. Therefore, experiments focused on detecting sub-GeV dark matter should seriously consider the possibility of observing this phenomenon. Statements of sensitivity indicate that the M-ToE, MIGCAM, GEODG, SENSEI, LIDINE and LINC experiments have the potential to discover this process. Among these, SENSEI has the capability to reach cross-sections stronger by four orders of magnitude when comparing in situ measurements with those using external sources. This paper proposes a method to produce the most connected pairs of qubit states
via an anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction system. It illustrates that an anti-Jaynes
Cummings interaction can lead to the transmission of one photon at a specific time
point, which is comparable to conventional Jaynes-Cummings interaction for a
micromaser system. Moreover, the anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction offers an
alternative for generating certain entangled states that are challenging to achieve
with the standard model. Notably, it provides a means to produce Rabi oscillations
in both the emitter and photon, thereby enabling the observation of Rabi effects
in both sides of the system. Finally, this study examines the relationship between
Rabi oscillations, entanglement, and photon transmission as the anti-Jaynes
Cummings interaction progresses. It shows that entanglement is necessary for photon
transmission and that Rabi oscillations of the emitter and photon occur
simultaneously when entanglement reaches its peak. This study delves into the
properties of emitter degrees of freedom and their connection to entanglement and
Rabi oscillations within the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model. It analyzes the distinct
behaviors of different operator mappings in this model and their influence on the
system's quantum states. This involves the comparison of various operator mappings
and their effects on the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, particularly in terms of entanglement and Rabi oscillations. It also explores the conserved properties of this model and their utility in understanding and predicting the system's dynamic evolution. This study further examines the influence of dissipation on the system's entanglement and Rabi oscillations, revealing that although dissipation may destroy entanglement and Rabi oscillations, the system can still exhibit non-classical characteristics and entanglement at specific time points despite the impact of dissipation. Finally, this study investigates the emittance of radiation from the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model as it interacts with its environment, showing that although dissipation may destroy entanglement and Rabi oscillations, the system can still emit non-classical photons and the emitter remaining in a near-pure state. This study concludes by highlighting the distinct behaviors of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model and its parallels with conventional quantum systems. This includes the transmission of radiation, entanglement, Rabi oscillations, and the emission of non-classical photons, which are all essential indicators of quantum behavior.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when signals are heavily distorted by noise. Current methods, such as Frederick's method and Schatz's method, are simple and effective but prone to inaccuracies in noisy signals. A more advanced deep learning approach, called Tiramisu, has been successfully applied in various image processing tasks and has now been modified to detect IBIs from ECG signals, significantly outperforming traditional methods with a significant 85% improvement. This novel application of Tiramisu has opened up new possibilities for using this model in clinical practice to improve the accuracy of IBI measurements. Tiramisu's unique structure, consisting of an encoder and decoder with skip connections, enables it to learn a complex and detailed representation of the ECG signal, allowing for more accurate detection of IBIs. Tiramisu's pre-activation and post-activation two-layer neural networks also contribute to its success in learning to detect IBIs. Tiramisu's performance has been evaluated on a comprehensive dataset of 1750 signal beats, demonstrating its superiority over traditional methods with a significant 85% improvement. This new approach is expected to provide more accurate early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. Related code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/prateek/skimirresnextwmamoofnet. Bhatt et al. concluded that Tiramisu is a highly versatile model that can be applied to various tasks and is resistant to different types of noise. This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing human body postures and movements. Currently, the most influential human pose and skeleton datasets rely on in-studio, two-dimensional, or pre-rendered animations. In contrast, HUMBI is based on a vast collection of 251,113 multiview images featuring real people engaging in a variety of outdoor activities, captured using multiple high-resolution cameras. Each image has been annotated with a detailed skeleton model and multiple human figures, enabling a rich set of semantic and geometric insights. Additionally, the dataset includes tracklets comprising long sequences of images, often featuring the same individuals in dynamic environments. These tracklets offer a valuable resource for developers looking to advance the representation and translation of multiview data. To stimulate progress in this area, we present a new evaluation benchmark centered on single-image linear transformation, skeleton transfer, and pose-based image synthesis tasks. Our results demonstrate that current approaches using conventional pose-based auto-decoders or transformer architectures achieve superior performance on these benchmarks. Despite the rising need for models in non-English languages, creating and training neural networks in every language is impractical due to data scarcity and training costs. Cross-lingual transfer has been proposed as a solution, but it is hampered by a lack of universal task representations. We propose that task representations based on neural networks can provide weak guidance for model-agnostic cross-lingual transfer. Our method uses these representations to locate similar tasks in target languages and allows existing model fine-tuning in those tasks. Our results show that even unsupervised target data is sufficient for successful transfer in sentiment analysis and question classification, significantly outperforming current methods in many languages. A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by introducing new techniques - Propagation in Color Space and Recursive Feature Alignment - to further improve video super-resolution quality. The first innovation applies propagation in the Color INERTIAL Frame, aiming to utilize information within the input video more effectively. The second involves improving feature alignment by aligning features recursively, rather than simultaneously, as employed in the BasicVSR method. Our results through experimental analysis on the LQ-Video dataset reveal a notable enhancement in PSNR, with the improved model achieving 0.53 and 0.46 dB improvement at x3 and x5 scaling factors respectively, alongside a considerable reduction in SSIM. Moreover, our model exhibits improved flexibility in video super-resolution, with the findings from NTREND dataset indicating a notable boost in SSIM and PSNR over the BasicVSR method. Our code is available online at https://github.com/Inria/BasicVSR++ for academic users. The model's performance in real-world scenarios has been demonstrated through video demos at https://basicvsr.inria.fr/demos.html. Substantial time savings have been achieved due to the efficiency of the model, with the effect observed in the demo videos at https://basicvsr.inria.fr/demos.html. Our model has been successfully tested on various test sets, including Vimeo-90p, LQ-Video, and Real-90p, with the model's generalization on inductive and transductive settings being analyzed through experimental investigation. A deep study into the effect of propagation steps on the performance of BasicVSR and our improved model has been conducted, with the findings from analysis by mean binary variance. Based on this, we introduced a novel technique - the Propagation Step Estimation - aiming to determine the optimal number of propagation steps. The test sets used for evaluation of our model and comparison with BasicVSR included Vimeo-90p, LQ-Video, and Real-90p. Our method has been successfully tested on various scaling factors, with the performance in x3 and x5 scaling factors being presented in the paper. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of applying model-based approaches with shared
representations to multi-task reinforcement learning settings. We demonstrate
theoretical and experimental findings showing that using shared representations
in model-free and model-based methods helps avoid the deterioration in learning
rate and performance due to task interference. Building on this insight, we
propose a novel model-based multi-task reinforcement learning algorithm called
MODULAR MBM (Modular Networks to Avoid Interference in Model-Based Multi-task
Reinforcement Learning). In this algorithm, shared networks process state and
action observations, while task-specific networks update their parameters by
performing policy updates based on reward functions. Our empirical evaluations
on diverse ATARI games reveal that MODULAR MBM significantly outperforms current
state-of-the-art multi-task reinforcement learning methods while significantly
reducing computational costs. Notably, this enhancement in performance comes
with minimal increases in computational overhead, particularly in terms of memory
requirements. Overall, our work contributes to the body of multi-task
reinforcement learning by showcasing the potential benefits and simplicity of
using shared representations in model-based methods. Additionally, our study
highlights the potential for model-based approaches to excel in practical,
at-scale gaming environments. The developed MODULAR MBM algorithm is now available
on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/amirgrabe/modular-mbm. MATLAB code for

allowing researchers to apply marker-based notation to manipulate morphisms 
and objects across various categories, regardless of their type. This approach 
has proven particularly useful in bicategories, where shadows help establish a 
connection between mapping out of a bicategory and the opposite of its 
category of morphism units. This relationship is shown to be precise in nature. 
Furthermore, several key properties of marks are demonstrated in relation to 
satisfying this condition. This concept is then applied to simulate marked 
versions of subcategories, where coproducts are replaced with shadows of such. 
Ultimately, this method is used to map out of the category of morphism units 
in a bicategory as a category with shadows, where the mapping preserves 1-cells. 
This approach is also tested on specific examples of groups and comonads. 
Lastly, a question is posed as to whether this technique can be extended to 
category theory itself. This method may have additional uses and applications 
that have yet to be discovered.

A new method, referred to as Deep Active Prediction (DAP), has been developed to enable autonomous robots to better plan and execute tasks by incorporating the robot's actions and perceptions. DAP introduces an innovative learning and decision-making framework that uses artificial neural networks. This approach forms part of a self-contained DAP system that integrates DAP as both a predictive and active learning model. Furthermore, DAP's performance was demonstrated through a series of simulated experiments involving navigation. These experiments revealed that DAP can significantly boost predictive accuracy and reduce uncertainty in robots' internal representations compared to a passive approach. Additionally, DAP was found to be more effective than existing active learning methods, including query-by-distribution and support query. Overall, DAP's integration is expected to greatly enhance the development of autonomous robots. Codes and the DAP2 demo are available online. Real-time analysis of event data from particle accelerators is crucial for making timely discoveries, particularly for experiments such as the COMET trilinear collider where a large volume of detector data poses significant processing challenges. Given the limited available bandwidth for data transmission from the detector to the central analysis system, data compression is a vital aspect of data management. Traditionally, compression methods focus on either removing redundant information or finding the most representative features of data. In this paper, we introduce a bicephalous convolutional autoencoder that simultaneously addresses both objectives by capturing primary features of the data while also removing correlated noise. TPC data's spatial symmetry is leveraged to reduce the input dimensionality to two dimensions, and various convolutional autoencoders are compared to optimize the compression process. By applying the best approach, a 30:1 compression ratio is achieved for 3D TPC data, enabling the successful transmission of reduced data to central systems for real-time analysis. Moreover, the introduced method's effectiveness in preserving physical signals and discarding noise is confirmed through multiple metrics, and its potential to adapt to various detectors and data types makes it a versatile tool for a wide range of particle physics experiments. Additionally, the code for the bicephalous convolutional autoencoder has been openly sourced for public use. This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective treatments for colon-cancer patients based on their unique immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the interactions between the patient's immune system and the colon cancer cells, with the Fokker-Planck equation governing the evolution of the probabilistic transition density. An optimal control problem is formulated to maximize the patient's survival time by administering the optimal treatment. Due to the FP equation's non-linearity, a time-symmetric variational problem is employed to facilitate numerical solutions. Consequently, a series of time-stamped control problems are obtained, enabling the development of customized treatment strategies for colon-cancer patients based on their individualized immune response. Two specific cases are numerically solved to illustrate the practical applications of the proposed framework. Furthermore, the proposed approach respects the patient's autonomy by ensuring that any obtained solution remains within the realm of existing medical treatments. An open-access computer code is available for reproducing the presented results. Additionally, the corresponding author can provide further information upon request. Among these types of helicity, the kinetic helicity, which is calculated as the dot product of the velocity vector and the cross product of the velocity and a spatial position vector, is particularly notable. However, the conservation of kinetic helicity has only been formally proven in specific cases, such as ideal magnetohydrodynamics, although numerous studies have provided evidence for its conservation in other systems through numerical simulations. In this study, we provide a strict mathematical proof that kinetic helicity remains constant over time for the compressible Euler equations. This proof can be adapted for certain dissipative models, such as the barotropic compressible Navier-Stokes equations with a constant density gradient. We further demonstrate that kinetic helicity is not conserved in flows with boundaries, but remains constant in unbounded flows. Finally, we conduct numerical simulations to illustrate conservation in scenarios with periodic and non-periodic flows. These experiments show that numerical methods can accurately predict kinetic helicity up to the round-off error. Nonetheless, we note that the order of convergence may vary depending on the location in space and time. Notably, the time at which we compute helicity is particularly significant and may limit the temporal convergence order. Ultimately, this proof provides evidence that kinetic helicity is conserved for a wide range of flows, but we also highlight the inherent dissipation inherent in certain types of flows. In order to further explore this dissipation, we conduct a detailed analysis of the error terms in the equations for kinetic helicity, which can be extended to a more general model of the barotropic compressible Navier-Stokes equations. Interestingly, the resulting error terms appear to be a dissipative force that can be bounded by a specific dissipation integral. Ultimately, this proof may pave the way for a more general theory of helicity conservation in fluid dynamics. A new type of x-ray amplifier is proposed, which would generate extremely intense, short pulses of x-rays. This "x-ray laser" relies on the unique properties of undulator free-electron laser oscillators, which produce a high-density seed radiation. This seed, comprised of fully coherent x-ray pulses, can be used to pump a long, excited gain medium, such as a laser ion, to produce higher-intensity x-ray pulses. Simulation results indicate that, assuming technological limitations are accounted for, an achievable level of intensity could be reached, which is far beyond current capabilities, reaching levels of 10 to the power of 14 Watts, or even higher, with x-ray pulse durations of approximately 50 attoseconds, at a wavelength of around 0.1 nanometers. This x-ray laser could have a multitude of applications, such as studying the fast dynamics of biological molecules, or generating high-energy x-rays to be directed at targets in astrophysical or laboratory plasmas. Furthermore, it could serve as a source for coherent x-ray scattering experiments, such as x-ray Thomson scattering, or for the creation of high-density, coherent x-ray beams to be used in x-ray free-electron lasers. Research has shown that incorporating additional information into node features can improve anomaly detection, but this approach has drawbacks, such as the potential for overfitting and the inability to model variations in network structures. To address these issues, we propose a method that uses an improved graph neural network to detect incidents on dynamic graphs. This method enhances incident detection while leveraging the underlying network structures. We also introduce a novel incident detection method based on spatial-temporal autoencoders that can identify incidents without requiring labeled data. Experimental results on real-world traffic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods. Specifically, our graph neural network achieves high accuracy with limited overfitting and outperforms existing methods. Additionally, our autoencoder method outperforms baseline approaches while producing notable reduction in dimensionality. Our code is publicly available. We examined how an imploding shock wave behaves in a medium with continuously increasing and decreasing density. Our model assumes a perfect gas with adiabatic index s and uses the ideal gas law for thermal energy and entropy calculations. By transforming the problem into a nonlinear equation involving a variable density flux, we demonstrated the existence of shock waves through various regularity estimates of its solutions. These estimates help us analyze the asymptotic behavior of solutions as time approaches infinity and their convergence towards a self-similar state. Additionally, our results reveal crucial limitations on the medium's density function to ensure smooth and single-valued solution trajectories. Our theoretical findings align with existing numerical simulation results. Furthermore, we explored the generalization of our model to include magnetic fields and offered potential directions for future research. Our study's main theoretical aspects have been published in a separate paper (Benououa et al., 2020). In contrast to other research on this topic, our work focuses on the medium's density as the primary driving force for solution impllosion, rather than using forcing functions or external field interactions. Our model's simplicity allows us to derive sharp asymptotic bounds and recover existing special case results, thereby highlighting their broader applicability. Our work also addresses the non-analytic nature of solution profiles by leveraging Hardy space theory and frequency domain estimates. Our analysis of solution behavior near the origin reveals the inherent discontinuities and "blow-ups" in solution trajectories, which we successfully overcome through the application of nonlinear approximation techniques and time-scale analysis. Our study also delves into the use of a specially designed real-frequency limit operator to derive explicit formulae for solution trajectories at all times and distances. The growing presence of intelligent systems powered by machine learning can be attributed to their superior performance in tackling complex tasks, particularly those involving little to no available information. While user-friendly interfaces and streamlined interaction methods have improved, many systems still fall short in providing understandable reasons for their actions and output predictions. This usability gap can be bridged by requirements engineering (RE) practitioners, who can ensure system developers incorporate the needs and expectations of novice users into the requirements. Specifically, we will demonstrate how RE can play a pivotal role in addressing user comprehension of machine learning-based systems by discussing the challenges, potential solutions, and future directions for incorporating explainability requirements. A concrete example illustrates the utility of practical guidelines suggested for capturing explainability needs. By abiding by these guidelines, system developers can facilitate user understanding, thereby enhancing the overall experience of interacting with intelligent systems. This is a preliminary position paper, and we welcome contributions from the community in the form of additional requirements, use cases, or responses to the questions posed throughout the rest of the paper. This will enable us to further explore the intersection of explainable AI and RE in future work. This position paper is a extension of and will be a chapter in a forthcoming book titled 'Artificial Intelligence and Requirements Engineering'. Accurate vertebra localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and treatment. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in low-dose CT scans) make this task even more challenging. To address these issues, a new and improved method has been developed to locate and identify vertebrae in CT images, even in difficult cases. This method works by first aligning and straightening the spine to its normal position, and then using a set of key parameters (e.g., rib positions, and center of mass of the sacrum and coccyx) that are estimated simultaneously to accurately position and identify the vertebrae. This method was tested and validated using a competitive evaluation protocol that includes 308 CT scans from two public datasets (LITS and SS-MSLC), and compared with six other state-of-the-art approaches. The results of this evaluation demonstrate that this new method achieves the highest overall area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (0.9536), significantly outperforming the other approaches in localizing and identifying vertebrae, especially in challenging cases. The proposed method has also shown its capability to robustly handle significant pathologies (e.g., compression fractures, fixation, and deformation) with only minor adjustments, and with only ten parameters to optimize. Therefore, this new method is suitable for automatic spine analysis in various medical applications. In contrast, I argue that deep mathematical knowledge is an obstacle to clear thinking, particularly in scientific inquiry. While mathematical structures are invaluable for pinpointing patterns, they fall short in capturing the essence of the world, blindening one to the very same patterns in reality. In contrast, a straightforward, almost naive approach to the world, unencumbered by elaborate mathematical concepts, allows for a more authentic and intuitive understanding. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-In-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction of magnetic flux cords. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The comparative study involves three scenarios: the MHD-AEPIC model, MHD alone, and fully kinetic Particle-In-Cell simulations. The examination of reconnection rates, magnetic rope topology, and adaptive model cutoff levels reveals notable similarities among the models. The MHD-AEPIC model demonstrates capability in detecting reconnection rates and magnetic island characteristics, even with minimal embedded kinetic regions, thereby validating its potential in studying magnetic reconnection and island coalescence processes. The integration of the MHD-AEPIC model with adaptive embedded kinetic elements promises a more efficient and feasible method for researching various magnetohydrodynamic and kinetic phenomena. The model's success sets a hopeful stage for utilizing it in studying intricate, complex physical systems where reconnection and other kinetic processes play a significant role. The report further had comparisons with PIC simulations, assessing reconnection island's structure and magnetic topology with and without adaptation. We propose a framework for a data structure called the program list, which enables efficient generation of ordered lists of values from query results, while maintaining their logical order. Our investigation of the program list reveals that current database systems fall short in this aspect, leading to suboptimal performance in applications requiring this functionality, such as sorting and ranking content in social media and online advertising. To address this limitation, we introduce Amanuensis, a data manager that utilizes a prepared statement cache and program list cache to enhance the performance of database-driven web applications, specifically those involving content management and blogging platforms. Our evaluation showcases the effectiveness of Amanuensis in improving cache hit rates and memory utilization, thereby leading to improved application performance and reduced memory consumption. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility and accuracy of our implementation, which is particularly useful in real-world scenarios for both developers and administrators. Our findings highlight the significance of program lists as a critical data element, while also revealing that current database systems fail to meet this need, thereby creating a notable gap in functionality that ultimately affects application performance and user experience. Conversely, by addressing this limitation, Amanuensis not only enhances the performance of database-driven applications but also closes the existing gap in functionality, thereby leading to improved user experience and ultimate success. Systematically evaluated from multiple angles, our solution has been rigorously tested to ensure the validity and accuracy of its results, which in turn document the effectiveness of our approach. To facilitate reproduction, we have openly shared the source code of our evaluation, which is readily accessible to the public. To achieve this goal, we developed Amanuensis, a training framework that guides developers through the design and implementation of program lists and associated cache management mechanisms. Our approach systematically addresses performance, efficiency, and adaptability, while also providing a clear design architecture and program cache management adaptation framework. By doing so, we demonstrated the feasibility and accuracy of our method, which in turn showcases the effectiveness of our approach, while also highlighting the challenges faced by developers in implementing program lists and caching mechanisms, particularly when working with content management and blogging platforms.
